senses.definition: To seal off (a military vehicle or facility).
senses.example: Before the storm hit, the commander ordered the crew to button up the tank and wait.

core.definition: To fasten all the buttons on a coat or shirt, or to finish something neatly and conclude it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'up', and 'button' has secondary stress. The t flaps, and the phrase links smoothly, sounding like 'buh-den-UHP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in the sense of keeping quiet it can sound sharp or dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'button up your coat' when it is cold, and 'button up the report' in a work setting to mean finish it cleanly. Informally, 'button up' can mean to stop talking, as in 'Button up and listen', which can sound rude. A natural reply to 'Button up your coat' is 'Good idea, it's freezing'.

distinctions.note: Zip up is used for garments with zippers, while button up is used for garments with buttons.
Fasten is a more formal and general word, while button up is the everyday choice for clothing and for finishing work.
Wrap up means to conclude something, often a meeting or project, while button up for clothing or more formally for finishing a document.

examples.everyday: Button up your jacket before you go out, because it's windy and cold.
examples.professional: Let's button up the budget by Friday so we can present it to finance.
examples.analytical: The author tries to button up the argument too neatly, leaving aside the counterevidence that complicates the thesis.

nuance.analogy: Buttoning up is like closing the last gap in a fence: it finishes the structure so nothing is left open.
common_mistakes: Saying 'button the coat up' without a clear object order; both 'button up your coat' and 'button your coat up' are used, but the first is more common.
Confusing 'button up' with 'button down', which means to fasten the collar of a shirt or to be conservative.

senses.definition: To believe (something, especially something implausible); to accept (a craze, fad, or notion) as valid.
senses.example: I don't buy into all this propaganda.

senses.definition: To buy stocks or shares of (a business).
senses.example: We bought into a local electrical firm.

core.definition: To believe in or accept an idea, claim, or plan, often without questioning it closely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on IN, with a lighter stress on buy. In fast American speech into often reduces to 'in-tuh,' so do not give it a full 'in-too' vowel every time.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can mean sincere acceptance, but in negative contexts it suggests someone was persuaded or naive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use buy into in workplace and political talk to mean accept a plan or belief, as in 'Does the team buy into the new strategy?' In negative contexts such as 'I don't buy it' or 'She bought into the hype,' it suggests skepticism or gullibility. It is informal but natural in meetings and everyday conversation. A typical reply is 'I'm not sure I buy into that.'

distinctions.note: Believe in is neutral and sincere, while buy into often implies that the belief was adopted under pressure or enthusiasm.
Fall for is stronger and implies being deceived, while buy into can describe accepting an idea without the sense of being tricked.

examples.everyday: My husband never bought into the idea of a smart thermostat, but now he loves it.
examples.professional: Leadership needs to buy into the new roadmap before we announce it to the whole department.
examples.analytical: Many citizens buy into the notion that markets always self-correct, even when the historical evidence is mixed.

nuance.analogy: It is like paying admission to a belief system: once you buy into it, you accept its terms.
nuance.etymology: From the verb buy combined with into, used figuratively in English to mean accept or believe.
common_mistakes: Using 'buy in' without 'to' when the object is an idea, which sounds unnatural.
Mistaking the idiom for a literal purchase, which can confuse listeners when used about a company or business investment.

senses.definition: By force of; by means of.
senses.example: He succeeded by dint of effort, not talent.

senses.definition: Because of; by reason of.

core.definition: As a result of, or by means of, a particular effort, force or factor; because of something's power or persistence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the content word 'dint', which rhymes with 'mint'. The 'of' reduces to a weak 'uhv', so don't pronounce a full 'of'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It credits a result to effort, persistence or a means, and sounds elevated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in formal writing, speeches and profiles, mostly for achievements: 'He passed the bar by dint of years of late-night study.' In everyday speech they usually say 'through' or 'thanks to'. It is rare in casual conversation.

distinctions.vs: by dint of vs. thanks to
distinctions.note: 'Thanks to' is everyday and can be positive or ironic; 'by dint of' is formal and stresses the effort or force that produced the result.

distinctions.vs: by dint of vs. by means of
distinctions.note: 'By means of' names a method or tool; 'by dint of' emphasizes the force, effort or persistence behind an outcome.

examples.everyday: We finished the basement by dint of a lot of weekends and a very patient spouse.
examples.professional: The team cut build time in half by dint of rewriting the caching layer and pruning old dependencies.
examples.analytical: Her argument, by dint of sheer logical discipline, survives objections that would sink a weaker thesis.

nuance.analogy: Like carving a path through rock: progress comes from steady pressure applied over time.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dynt, 'a blow' or 'stroke'.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'of' and saying 'by dint hard work'; the phrase requires 'of'.
Pronouncing 'dint' like 'dent' or 'dined'.

senses.definition: A person who exhibits the traits of bad spelling or bad handwriting or both.

core.definition: A person who writes or spells badly, or has poor handwriting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KOG, and do not stress the first syllable 'cac-'. The final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel, like 'fur' said quickly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It mocks someone's careless or incorrect writing and is usually used with a touch of scorn.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation; it appears in literary writing, academic discussion of language, or humorous commentary. It is much more formal than saying someone is a bad speller. In everyday speech, people say 'bad speller' or 'terrible handwriting' instead.

distinctions.note: A calligrapher is skilled at beautiful handwriting, while a cacographer writes badly.
A typo is a single slip, while a cacographer is a person who habitually writes or spells poorly.
Illiterate means unable to read or write at all, while a cacographer can read and write but does so badly.

examples.professional: Our editor is a patient reader, but she admits she was once a cacographer on every report she wrote in college.
examples.analytical: The critic treats the letter writer as a cacographer whose errors reveal a hurried, unlettered mind.

nuance.analogy: A cacographer's handwriting is like a map drawn in a hurry: the lines are there, but no one can easily follow them.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kakos, 'bad', and graphein, 'to write'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'calligrapher', which means someone with beautiful handwriting.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'KAK-uh-grafer'.

senses.definition: A complete assembly, consisting of an artillery tube and a breech mechanism, firing mechanism or base cap, which is a component of a gun, howitzer or mortar, which may include muzzle appendages.
senses.example: The museum restored a nineteenth-century bronze cannon that still sits on its original wooden carriage.

senses.definition: Any similar device for shooting material out of a tube.
senses.example: water cannon; glitter cannon; confetti cannon; potato cannon

senses.definition: A bone of a horse’s leg, between the fetlock joint and the knee or hock.
senses.example: The farrier said the horse had a small crack in its cannon bone.

senses.definition: A rolled and filleted loin of meat.
senses.example: a canon of beef or lamb

senses.definition: A cannon bit.
senses.example: The trainer switched the bridle to a cannon bit with rollers for the young gelding.

senses.definition: A hollow cylindrical piece carried by a revolving shaft, on which it may, however, revolve independently.
senses.example: The engineer replaced the worn cannon on the spindle so the gear would turn freely.

senses.definition: A pickpocket.
senses.example: The old detective warned tourists that a cannon was working the crowd near the station.

senses.definition: An autocannon.
senses.example: The helicopter's nose-mounted cannon fired a short burst at the target vehicle.

senses.definition: A carom.
senses.example: In English billiards, a cannon is when one’s cue ball strikes the other player’s cue ball and the red ball on the same shot; and it is worth two points.

senses.definition: The arm of a player who can throw well.
senses.example: He’s got a cannon out in right.

senses.definition: A piece which moves horizontally and vertically like a rook but captures another piece by jumping over a different piece in the line of attack.
senses.example: In xiangqi, the cannon can only capture by jumping over exactly one piece.

senses.definition: (historical) A large muzzle-loading artillery piece.
senses.example: Union engineers hauled a massive smoothbore cannon up the hill before dawn.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A cylindrical item of plate armor protecting the arm, particularly one of a pair of such cylinders worn with a couter, the upper cannon protecting the upper arm and the lower cannon protecting the forearm.
senses.example: The knight's steel cannon guarded his forearm while the couter protected the elbow joint.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To bombard with cannons.
senses.example: Enemy ships cannoned the coastal fort through the night until the walls crumbled.

senses.definition: To fire something, especially spherical, rapidly.
senses.example: The ball machine cannoned tennis balls toward the practice wall every few seconds.

senses.definition: To collide or strike violently, especially so as to glance off or rebound.
senses.example: The runaway shopping cart cannoned off the car door and bounced into the curb.

senses.definition: To play the carom billiard shot; to strike two balls with the cue ball.
senses.example: The white cannoned off the red onto the pink.

core.definition: A large, heavy gun, usually mounted on wheels or a carriage, that fires heavy shells or solid balls, especially in historical or military use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the second to a light uhn: KAN-uhn. Avoid the Spanish-style 'kah-NYOHN' or a long a sound in the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts, though it evokes war and violence in military discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cannon for historical artillery, such as Civil War cannons in parks and museums, and in sports or fireworks talk. As a verb, cannon means a ball or object striking something and bouncing off, as in 'The ball cannoned off the post,' which is common in American sports reporting. In American pool, however, people usually say 'carom' rather than 'cannon.'

distinctions.note: Gun is the general word for any firearm, while cannon is specifically a large, heavy artillery piece.
Canon is a homophone meaning a rule, a standard, or an official list, so the spelling must be chosen carefully.

examples.everyday: The kids climbed all over the old cannon at the fort, pretending they were defending the wall.
examples.professional: Our contractor confirmed the cannon on the replica is decorative and cannot be fired for safety reasons.
examples.analytical: The adoption of rifled cannon in the nineteenth century transformed siege warfare by making fortress walls far more vulnerable.

nuance.analogy: A cannon is like a heavy hammer on the battlefield: it strikes from a distance and can break down walls that stronger people cannot climb over.
nuance.etymology: From Italian cannone, an augmentative of canna, meaning tube or reed, from Latin canna.
common_mistakes: Confusing cannon with canon, which means a rule, a standard, or a list of books.
Confusing cannon with canyon, which is a deep valley.
Stressing the second syllable or saying it like 'kah-NYOHN'.

cannon.etymology: Attested from around 1400 as Middle English *canon*, *canoun*, from Old French *canon*, from Italian *cannone*, from Latin *canna*, from Ancient Greek *κάννα* (“reed”), from *𒄀* (“reed”), from *𒄀𒈾* (for more, see *cane*).

senses.definition: Testing what a model is able to do, often in a specific risky domain.
senses.example: Before release, the lab ran a capability evaluation to see whether the model could assist with malware writing.

core.definition: Testing an AI model to find out what it can do, especially dangerous abilities, before release.

pronunciation.tip: The main stresses are on BIL in capability and on AY in evaluation, with a secondary stress on VAL. The vowel in the second syllable of evaluation is a reduced 'ih,' not a full 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized term in AI safety and policy, and it describes measurement rather than praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in AI labs, safety teams, and policy discussions use capability evaluation as a standard phrase, often shortened to 'capability evals.' It is not used in everyday speech. Colleagues might say 'We are running capability evals before the release,' and a natural reply is 'Sounds good, what are the thresholds?'

distinctions.note: A safety evaluation checks how a model behaves or whether it causes harm, while a capability evaluation checks what the model is able to do at all.
A benchmark is a fixed test set with a standard score, while a capability evaluation can be a broader investigation that includes custom prompts and elicitation methods.
Red teaming is adversarial testing by people trying to make the model fail, while a capability evaluation measures the model's potential ability in a specified domain.

examples.everyday: My friend who works at an AI lab says they spend weeks on capability evals before anything ships.
examples.professional: Before we release the model, the safety team needs the capability evaluation results for cyber and bio tasks.
examples.analytical: A capability evaluation can establish that a model can perform a dangerous task, but a negative result does not prove absence, since weak elicitation may hide latent ability.

nuance.analogy: A capability evaluation is like a stress test on a bridge, measuring its maximum load so engineers know what it can safely carry before opening it to traffic.
nuance.etymology: Capability comes from capable, from Late Latin capabilis, and evaluation comes from evaluate, from French evaluer, to find the value of.
common_mistakes: Treating a failed capability evaluation as proof that the model lacks the ability, when the test prompts may not have elicited it.
Confusing capability evaluation with safety evaluation, which asks a different question about behavior and harm.

conversation.text: A capability evaluation measures what a model can do, including skills that could be dangerous.
Capability evaluations before release help decide what safeguards a model needs.
A weak prompt can make a capability evaluation underestimate what the model can really do.

senses.definition: A piece or point of land, extending beyond the adjacent coast into a sea or lake; a promontory; a headland.
senses.example: The lighthouse stands at the tip of the cape, where fog rolls in every morning.

senses.definition: A sleeveless garment or part of a garment, hanging from the neck over the back, arms, and shoulders.
A superhero.
senses.example: The comic book's newest cape rescued the stranded children from the burning bridge.

senses.definition: To incite or attract (a bull) to charge a certain direction, by waving a cape.
senses.example: The matador capes the bull toward the left side of the ring to set up his pass.

senses.definition: To skin (an animal, or particularly the head and shoulders of an animal, especially a deer), for taxidermy.
senses.example: The taxidermist capes the deer's head and shoulders before sending the hide to the tannery.

senses.definition: To defend or praise, especially that which is unworthy.
senses.example: Some commentators still cape for the boss's careless decisions, insisting he was merely misunderstood.

senses.definition: To cover (as) with or like a cape.
senses.example: Fresh snow capes the mountain peaks, glittering white under the winter sun.

senses.definition: To head or point; to keep a course.
senses.example: The ship capes southwest by south.

core.definition: A sleeveless cloak that hangs from the neck over the shoulders and back, worn for warmth, style, or costume.

pronunciation.tip: Use the long a of day and a clear final p. Do not shorten it to the vowel of cap, because the word differs from cap by its vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. A cape can be practical, fashionable, or playful, depending on the setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cape for a sleeveless cloak in fashion, rain gear, and Halloween or theater costumes. In US slang, a cape can also mean a superhero, as in 'the cape movies,' which is informal and playful. Cape is also used in place names such as Cape Cod, where it refers to a landform.

distinctions.note: A cloak is usually longer and heavier, often with a hood or closure at the front, while a cape is shorter and has no front closure.
A poncho is a blanket-like garment with a hole for the head, while a cape hangs from the shoulders and is open at the front.
A shawl is draped loosely over the shoulders and arms, while a cape is a fuller, sleeveless garment that hangs from the neck.

examples.everyday: My son wore a red cape to the Halloween party and wouldn't take it off all night.
examples.professional: The event team ordered branded rain capes for the outdoor summit, since the forecast looked wet.
examples.analytical: In the portrait, the cape falls in heavy folds that suggest the subject's authority and self-confidence.

nuance.analogy: A cape is like a blanket draped over the shoulders with no sleeves to fill.
nuance.etymology: From French cape, from Old Provençal capa, from Latin cappa, a hooded cloak.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing cape with the short a of cap, which makes the word sound like a hat.
Confusing cape with cave, which has the same vowel but means an underground space.

cape.etymology: From Middle English *cape*, *gappe*, *cap*, from Old French *cap* (“cape, headland”), from Latin *caput* (“head”).

senses.definition: Castle-like: built or shaped like a castle; usually, specifically, having castellations (crenellations).
senses.example: The tourists photographed the castellated towers of the medieval fortress on the hilltop.

senses.definition: Having grooves or recesses on an upper face. Castellated holes on the edge of a printed circuit board.
senses.example: Engineers added castellated holes along the edge of the circuit board so modules could be soldered flat.

senses.definition: Castled: having or furnished with castles.
Synonym of enclosed, when used for fountains, cisterns, &c.
senses.example: The old stone cistern was castellated, so rainwater stayed protected from leaves and debris.

senses.definition: (rare) Housed or kept in a castle.
senses.example: For centuries the royal archives were castellated within the northern fortress, away from the city.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Built with battlements like a castle; in electronics, having notches or half-holes cut along an edge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, not a full 'ah'. The ending '-ated' is said 'ay-tid' with the last vowel very short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing architecture or hardware; slightly decorative or romantic in literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly for medieval-style towers, walls, and buildings, or for the notched parapet on top of them. In electronics, engineers use it for half-holes along the edge of a circuit board that are soldered to a carrier board. In everyday speech, people say 'a building with notches on top' or 'a castle-style wall' instead.

distinctions.note: Crenellated is the more common architectural term for a parapet with alternating raised and lowered sections, so it is often used interchangeably with castellated.
Castled means having or furnished with castles; castellated describes the battlement-like shape or notches, not the presence of castles.

examples.everyday: That old stone building downtown has a castellated top, like something out of a fairy tale.
examples.professional: The PCB has castellated holes along the edge, so we can solder the module straight onto the carrier board.
examples.analytical: The castellated walls of the fortress signal both defense and aristocratic display, making the architecture a statement of power.

nuance.analogy: Like the notched top of a rook in a chess set.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin castellatus, from castellum 'small fortress', a diminutive of castrum 'fortified camp'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'cas-tel-AY-tid'; the stress is on the first syllable.
Confusing it with 'castellan' (a castle's warden), which is a different word.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of catalog.
senses.example: She will catalog the donated books before the sale opens Friday.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of catalog.
senses.example: She will catalog the donated books before the sale opens Friday.

core.definition: A complete list of items, such as products, books, or library holdings, usually arranged in a systematic order.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel reduces to 'uh'. The final syllable rhymes with 'dog', using the cot-caught vowel, and ends with a clear hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical word for lists and inventories.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell this word 'catalog', while British writers use 'catalogue'; use 'catalog' in American writing, including for the verb. Americans use it for product catalogs, library catalogs, course catalogs, and online shopping. In speech, they usually say 'the catalog' or 'the online catalog' for a list of items.

distinctions.note: Catalogue is the British spelling, so avoid it in American writing and documents.
A list is simpler and less formal and need not be systematic, while a catalog is a more organized, comprehensive record.
A directory lists people, organizations, or contact information, while a catalog lists items for sale or in a collection.

examples.everyday: Can you check the online catalog to see if they still carry that lamp in blue?
examples.professional: We need to catalog every dataset before we load it into the warehouse so the team can find it later.
examples.analytical: Linnaeus's attempt to catalog the species of nature shaped the modern system of biological classification.

nuance.analogy: A catalog is like the index of a library: a systematic map that tells you what is there and where to find it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin catalogus, from Greek katalogos 'list, register', from katalegein 'to enumerate'.
common_mistakes: Writing the British spelling 'catalogue' in American documents.
Pronouncing the middle 'a' as a full 'ah' instead of a reduced vowel.
Misspelling the verb forms: 'cataloging' with one l is the American spelling, not 'catalogueing'.

senses.definition: In a catastrophic manner, or to a catastrophic extent; disastrously.
senses.example: The startup's servers failed catastrophically during the product launch, taking the whole site offline.

senses.definition: To an extreme degree.

core.definition: In a disastrous way, to a degree that causes serious damage or complete failure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress STRAH, the same syllable as in catastrophic. Pronounce the final -ly as a clear 'lee' sound, and do not add an extra syllable before it.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes damage or failure, although informal speakers sometimes use it to emphasize how bad something is.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'catastrophically' in news, technical reports and workplace discussions to describe failures that are severe and sudden. In casual speech, it is used for emphasis, as in 'I got catastrophically lost,' which is humorous but still dramatic. Use it sparingly, because it sounds strong in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: The two words are close in meaning, but 'disastrously' is slightly more common in everyday speech, while 'catastrophically' is stronger and more technical.
'Badly' is neutral and general, while 'catastrophically' signals severe, large-scale failure.

examples.everyday: I thought the cake would be fine, but it burned catastrophically in the oven.
examples.professional: The migration failed catastrophically when the database schema changed without warning.
examples.analytical: Without safeguards, the system fails catastrophically rather than degrading gracefully.

nuance.analogy: Like a dam that bursts instead of leaking, the system fails all at once instead of slowly losing performance.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'catastrophic' with the adverb suffix -ally, which is pronounced -li in American speech.
common_mistakes: Using 'catastrophically' for small problems, which sounds exaggerated.
Confusing it with 'catastrophical,' an older and less common form that Americans rarely use.

senses.definition: A new or recent member of a Greek monastic religious order; a caloyer.
senses.example: The young novice joined the cenobite community on Mount Athos as a new brother.

senses.definition: A monk who lives in a religious community, rather than in solitude.
A torturous demon creature made famous by the Hellraiser series.
senses.example: In the horror film, the cenobite stalked the house, its chains rattling through the dark hallway.

core.definition: A monk who lives in a religious community with others under a shared rule, rather than alone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the reduced middle syllable be a quick 'uh'. The ending rhymes with 'bite', not 'bit'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and religious. In popular culture, the word also names a horror-film demon, but in ordinary use it means a monk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'cenobite' in daily life; they would say 'monk' or 'monastic'. The word appears in religious history and theology to contrast community life with hermits. Most Americans who know the word first from the Hellraiser films are thinking of the demons, which is a different sense.

distinctions.note: A hermit lives alone in solitude; a cenobite lives in a community with others under a shared rule.
'Monk' is the general term and can include hermits; 'cenobite' specifically means a monk who lives in community.

examples.everyday: The monks at that abbey all live together, so I guess you'd call them cenobites.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit's history report describes early Egyptian cenobites who organized shared work and worship.
examples.analytical: Pachomius's rule made the cenobite life a structured communal discipline rather than a solitary search for God.

nuance.analogy: A cenobite is like a monk living in a shared house with a common schedule, while a hermit lives alone in a cabin in the woods.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin coenobita, from Greek koinobios, 'living in common,' from koinos, 'common,' and bios, 'life'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'hermit'; a cenobite lives in community, not alone.
Using it to mean the Hellraiser horror creatures in ordinary conversation; in most contexts it means a religious monk.

cenobite.etymology: From Old French *cenobite* or Ecclesiastical Latin *coenobīta*, from *coenobium*, from Ancient Greek *κοινόβιον* (“community life, convent”), from *κοινός* (“common”) + *βίος* (“life”).

senses.definition: The hollow bed of running waters; the bed of the sea or other body of water.
senses.example: The water coming out of the waterwheel created a standing wave in the channel.

senses.definition: The natural or man-made deeper course through a reef, bar, bay, or any shallow body of water.
senses.example: A channel was dredged to allow ocean-going vessels to reach the city.

senses.definition: The navigable part of a river.
senses.example: We were careful to keep our boat in the channel.

senses.definition: A narrow body of water between two land masses.
senses.example: The English Channel lies between France and England.

senses.definition: Something through which another thing passes; a means of conveying or transmitting.
senses.example: The news was conveyed to us by different channels.

senses.definition: An ion channel: pore-forming proteins located in a cell membrane that allow specific ions to pass through.
senses.example: Researchers used patch-clamp recordings to measure how the potassium channel in the cell membrane opened.

senses.definition: A gutter; a groove, as in a fluted column.
senses.example: The carved stone column had a deep channel running down its length.

senses.definition: A structural member with a cross section shaped like a squared-off letter C.
senses.example: The contractor bolted a steel channel to the wall to support the shelving.

senses.definition: A connection between initiating and terminating nodes of a circuit.
senses.example: The guard-rail provided the channel between the downed wire and the tree.

senses.definition: The narrow conducting portion of a MOSFET transistor.
senses.example: Increasing the gate voltage widens the channel and lets more current flow through the transistor.

senses.definition: The part that connects a data source to a data sink.
senses.example: A channel stretches between them.

senses.definition: A path for conveying electrical or electromagnetic signals, usually distinguished from other parallel paths.
senses.example: We are using one of the 24 channels.

senses.definition: A single path provided by a transmission medium via physical separation, such as by multipair cable.
senses.example: The channel is created by bonding the signals from these four pairs.

senses.definition: A single path provided by a transmission medium via spectral or protocol separation, such as by frequency or time-division multiplexing.
senses.example: Their call is being carried on channel 6 of the T-1 line.

senses.definition: A specific radio frequency or band of frequencies, usually in conjunction with a predetermined letter, number, or codeword, and allocated by international agreement.
senses.example: KNDD is the channel at 107.7 MHz in Seattle.

senses.definition: A specific radio frequency or band of frequencies used for transmitting television.
senses.example: NBC is on channel 11 in San Jose.

senses.definition: The portion of a storage medium, such as a track or a band, that is accessible to a given reading or writing station or head.
senses.example: This chip in this disk drive is the channel device.

senses.definition: The part of a turbine pump where the pressure is built up.
senses.example: The liquid is pressurized in the lateral channel.

senses.definition: A distribution channel.
senses.example: The company sells its software through a reseller channel rather than directly to customers.

senses.definition: A particular area for conversations on an IRC or similar network, analogous to a chat room and often dedicated to a specific topic.
senses.example: Several developers hung out in the Python channel to help newcomers debug their code.

senses.definition: A psychic or medium who takes on the personality of a spirit and conveys messages from them.
senses.example: The woman claimed to be a channel who could speak with her late husband.

senses.definition: The wale of a sailing ship which projects beyond the gunwale and to which the shrouds attach via the chains. One of the flat ledges of heavy plank bolted edgewise to the outside of a vessel, to increase the spread of the shrouds and carry them clear of the bulwarks.
senses.example: The sailors checked the channels for loose chains before the ship set out.

senses.definition: (historical) A means of delivering up-to-date Internet content via a push mechanism.
senses.example: The startup's push channel delivered headlines to subscribers' desktops every morning, years before smartphones.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To make or cut a channel or groove in.
senses.example: Erosion had channeled the rainwater into deep grooves across the limestone surface.

senses.definition: To direct or guide along a desired course.
senses.example: We will channel the traffic to the left with these cones.

senses.definition: To serve as a medium for.
senses.example: She was channeling the spirit of her late husband, Seth.

senses.definition: To follow as a model, especially in a performance.
senses.example: He was trying to channel President Reagan, but the audience wasn't buying it.

core.definition: A means or route through which information, communication, or products are passed, such as a TV station or sales outlet.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel in the first syllable is a short 'a' as in 'cat', not 'ee' or 'ay'. Stress falls on CHAN, and the final syllable is a light 'uhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a route or medium without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use channel for TV and radio stations, for sales outlets, and for official routes, as in 'through the proper channels'. Saying 'I watched it on channel 5' is everyday talk. In business, 'sales channels' and 'distribution channels' are standard. The verb 'channel' means to direct or guide something through a route and is common in work talk.

distinctions.note: A network is a group of connected stations or people; a channel is one specific station or route within that system.
A route is a path for travel; a channel is a route for information, communication, or distribution.

examples.everyday: I usually catch the local news on channel 7 before dinner.
examples.professional: We sell through three channels: direct sales, regional distributors, and online marketplaces.
examples.analytical: In classical Christian thought, grace flows through the channels of sacrament and Scripture.

nuance.analogy: Like a pipe that carries water from one place to another, a channel carries information or goods along a set route.
nuance.etymology: From Old French chanel, from Latin canalis, a pipe or conduit.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as 'ee' from the spelling 'channel', as in 'cheen-uhl'.
Using channel for a single contact; it refers to a route or medium, so say 'a contact' or 'a source' for one person.

channel.etymology: From Middle English *chanel* (also as *canel*, *cannel*, *kanel*), a borrowing from Old French *chanel*, *canel*, from Latin *canālis* (“groove; canal; channel”).

senses.definition: In a chaotic manner.

core.definition: In a disorderly, confused way, with no clear plan or order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the AH syllable, the same as in chaotic. The ending '-ically' is pronounced 'ik-lee' with only two syllables after the stress, not four.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it describes disorder or confusion in how something happens.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chaotically to describe how people or events move, such as a crowd rushing a store or a meeting running out of control. It is common in everyday speech and news reports. It is more natural than 'in a chaotic manner', which sounds stiff.

distinctions.note: Randomly stresses lack of pattern, while chaotically stresses confusion and disorder in how something happens.

examples.everyday: The crowd pushed toward the stage chaotically when the doors finally opened.
examples.professional: The migration ran chaotically because nobody had documented the rollback plan.
examples.analytical: Her argument moved chaotically between three unrelated examples, so the thesis never came into focus.

nuance.analogy: Like a shopping cart with a bad wheel that veers in every direction.
nuance.etymology: From chaotic plus the adverb suffix -ally, ultimately from Greek khaos.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the final syllable instead of the AH syllable.
Saying 'chaotical' with an extra syllable; the adverb form is 'chaotically'.

senses.definition: In a chary manner.

core.definition: Cautiously and with reserve, holding back from trust, praise or commitment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, CHAIR, and keep the r rhotic. The middle vowel is short, and the final -ly is pronounced ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it suggests reserve or distrust.
nuance.usage_note: Charily is rare in speech and appears mostly in writing or literary prose. Americans more often say cautiously, warily or carefully. Use it to describe holding back from giving trust, praise or money.

distinctions.note: Warily stresses alertness to danger, while charily stresses holding back, especially from giving trust, praise or money.
Cautiously is common and neutral in everyday speech, while charily is formal and literary.

examples.professional: The manager spoke charily about the budget, since the numbers were still unconfirmed.
examples.analytical: The historian reads official records charily, aware that each document reflects the interests of its writers.

nuance.analogy: Like someone testing thin ice with each step, charily means moving forward only with careful, measured steps.
nuance.etymology: From chary (Old English cearig, careful, anxious) plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing charily with charitably, because the spellings look similar.
Pronouncing chary with two long syllables; it sounds like CHAIR-ee.

senses.definition: A gift or power of leadership or authority.
senses.example: The leader has his charisma.

senses.definition: The capacity to inspire devotion or enthusiasm; personal charm.
senses.example: the charisma of a popular actor

senses.definition: A gift or power bestowed upon a person by the Holy Spirit; a grace.
senses.example: Paul describes charisma as a gift of the Spirit given for the good of the church.

core.definition: A powerful personal quality that draws others to you and makes them trust, admire, or follow you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, RIZ. The first sound is a k, not the ch of 'chair', because the word comes from Greek.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a compliment for a person who is easy to follow or admire.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use charisma for a person's natural appeal, especially leaders, speakers, and celebrities. You might say, 'She has a lot of charisma' or 'He's got charisma.' In job reviews and news writing it is a common and admiring word.

distinctions.note: Charm is pleasant and warm, often in social settings, while charisma is stronger and tends to inspire loyalty or followers.
Charisma is secular personal appeal, while charism is a theological term for a gift from God.

examples.everyday: My cousin is so funny, he's got charisma even at a family barbecue.
examples.professional: The manager's charisma helped rally the team through a difficult product launch.
examples.analytical: Weber distinguished charismatic authority from traditional and legal-rational forms, grounding it in a leader's perceived extraordinary gifts.

nuance.analogy: Charisma is like a warm light that draws people in without any effort.
nuance.etymology: From Greek charisma, favor or gift of grace, from charis, grace.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch as in 'chair'; it is a hard k sound.
Using charisma for someone who is merely likable; it implies a stronger pull or influence.

charisma.etymology: From Ancient Greek *χᾰ́ρῐσμᾰ* (“grace, favour, gift”), from *χᾰρῐ́ζομαι* (“to show favor”), from *χᾰ́ρῐς* (“grace”), from the same root as *χαίρω* (“to be happy”).

senses.definition: To decrease the value or price of; to make cheaper.
senses.example: Constant discounts and coupons can cheapen a brand's image in customers' minds.

senses.definition: To make vulgar.
To become cheaper.
senses.example: Prices for the used laptops cheapened sharply once the new models arrived.

core.definition: To make something seem less valuable, dignified, or respected, or to lower its price or quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, CHEE. The final -en is a weak syllable that sounds like 'un,' not a full 'pen.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies that something valuable has lost dignity or worth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use cheapen when something meaningful is made to look worthless, such as through commercialization or careless treatment. It works both figuratively and, less often, literally. For simply lowering a price, Americans more often say lower or reduce.

distinctions.note: Devalue is more formal and often used for money or economic worth, while cheapen is about losing dignity or meaning.
Degrade is harsher and can imply moral or physical damage, while cheapen implies a loss of value or respect.
Lower is neutral about price and quality, while cheapen carries a sense of loss.

examples.everyday: Don't cheapen the wedding with bad music; people will remember the food and the friends.
examples.professional: Heavy discounting could cheapen our brand, so let's protect the premium price.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that market logic can cheapen love by reducing it to an exchange of goods.

nuance.analogy: Cheapening something is like polishing a silver spoon with sandpaper: it looks the same from far away but loses its shine up close.
nuance.etymology: From cheap, from Old English ceap meaning 'trade, price,' plus the verb suffix -en.
common_mistakes: Using cheapen for simply lowering a price in neutral contexts, where lower or reduce is more natural.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a full vowel, as in 'CHEE-pen.'

senses.definition: To announce or record one's own arrival at a hotel, airport etc.
senses.example: We got to the hotel last night and checked in at the front desk.

senses.definition: To verify a person's information and record their arrival, such as at a hotel, airport, etc.
senses.example: The clerk checked us in at the front desk.

senses.definition: To contact another person in order to keep the other person informed of one's situation.
senses.example: Kelly has to check in with her parole officer today.

senses.definition: To return (a book to a library, source code to a repository, etc.).
senses.example: Please check in your library books before the holiday so you avoid late fees.

senses.definition: To visit in order to see how someone is doing.
senses.example: I just wanted to check in after your accident. How are you recovering?

senses.definition: To enter solitary confinement at one's own request for protection from other prisoners.
senses.example: After receiving threats inside the yard, he asked to check in for his own safety.

senses.definition: To send somebody to solitary confinement; to make somebody be admitted to solitary confinement.
senses.example: The warden decided to check him in after the fight broke out in the cafeteria.

senses.definition: To integrate new revisions into the public or master version of a file in a version control system.
senses.example: Before the release, the developer will check in the final patch to the main branch.

senses.definition: To tap on, to touch in, to tap in (to use a smartcard to start a public transport journey)
senses.example: Remember to check in with your transit card at the station turnstile before boarding.

core.definition: To register your arrival at a hotel or airport, or to contact someone to report your situation or progress.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrasal verb, the particle in gets the main stress, so say chek IN. Don't give both words equal stress, because the particle carries the emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a routine, practical phrase used in daily life and work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans check in at hotels, airports, and doctors' offices, and they also check in with a colleague or family member to say they are okay. As a noun, check-in is written with a hyphen. A natural reply to a message is Thanks for checking in, or I'll check in later.

distinctions.note: Check out means leave a hotel or inspect something, while check in means arrive and register.
Check into is used for a specific place, like a hospital or hotel, while check in is more general and can be used with with or on.

collocations: check in at the front desk

examples.everyday: I'll check in with you tonight after I get to the hotel.
examples.professional: Please check in with me before you start the migration tomorrow morning.
examples.analytical: To check in is to renew a connection, showing the other party that the relationship continues.

nuance.analogy: Like signing the sheet at the door of a meeting to show you have arrived.
common_mistakes: Saying I checked to the hotel instead of I checked in at the hotel
Mixing up check in and check out when you are arriving or leaving

conversation.text: We can't check in to the hotel until three.
I'm just checking in to see how you're feeling.
I'm going to check in this suitcase, it's too big for the cabin.
You can check in online twenty-four hours before your flight.
Check-in is at three, but we can leave our bags early.

senses.definition: Divided into a grid of squares of alternating colors or shades, or into light and dark patches.
senses.example: That is a checkered tablecloth.

senses.definition: Changeable; inconsistent; having variations or uncertainty; marked by many problems or failures.
senses.example: Her checkered career includes stints as a bank teller, a failed startup, and a successful consultancy.

core.definition: Marked by ups and downs, failures, or inconsistency; not steady or successful throughout.

pronunciation.tip: There are two syllables, with stress on the first, CHEK. The middle vowel is a reduced American 'er' sound, so do not say 'chek-EE-ird.'

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, suggesting a history of problems or mixed results. It is mild and often used in news or professional writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mostly in the set phrases 'checkered past' and 'checkered career' for someone with a mixed or troubled history. For the literal pattern, Americans say 'checkered tablecloth' or 'checkered flag.' In British English the spelling is 'chequered,' so use 'checkered' in American writing.

distinctions.note: Spotty means uneven in quality over a short period, as with spotty Wi-Fi, while checkered suggests a long history of ups and downs.
Varied is neutral and describes different kinds of results, while checkered carries a negative sense of failure or trouble.
Chequered is the British spelling, so American writing uses checkered.

examples.everyday: He's got a checkered past, but he's been doing great since he got sober.
examples.professional: The team's delivery record is checkered, with two major launches on time and three that slipped badly.
examples.analytical: Her checkered record as a policymaker makes it hard to judge how much she actually shaped the reforms.

nuance.analogy: Like a checkerboard, where light and dark squares alternate, so the record swings between good and bad.
nuance.etymology: From 'check,' a square pattern, from Old French eschequier, 'chessboard.'
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'chequered' in American writing.
Using 'checkered' for a single mistake; it describes a long mixed history, not one error.
patterns: (usually before a noun) a checkered past/history

senses.definition: A person skilled in chronology.

core.definition: A person who is an expert in chronology, the science of arranging events and dates in time order.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'NAH'. The first syllable is weak, so 'chrono' sounds more like 'kruh' than 'kroh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It describes a specialist and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Chronologist is rare in everyday American English and appears mainly in academic history, archaeology, and scholarly writing. Americans more often say historian, archivist, or 'someone who dates events'. Use it when you specifically mean a scholar who establishes the order and dates of events.

distinctions.note: A historian interprets the meaning and causes of past events, while a chronologist focuses on establishing their exact dates and sequence.
An archivist preserves and organizes records, while a chronologist uses records to build a timeline.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a bit of a chronologist and can name the exact year of every family wedding.
examples.professional: The research team hired a chronologist to check the dates on the project's timeline.
examples.analytical: As a chronologist, she argues that the two accounts cannot both be correct about the sequence of events.

nuance.analogy: A chronologist is like a librarian for time, placing each event on the right shelf of the calendar.
nuance.etymology: From chronology, from Greek chronos (time) and logos (word, account), with the agent suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Using chronologist for someone who simply tells time or owns a clock.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'kroh' instead of a weak 'kruh'.

senses.definition: To draw the smallest circle or higher-dimensional sphere that has (a polyhedron, polygon, etc.) in its interior.
senses.example: Students learned to circumscribe each triangle with a circle that passes through all three vertices.

senses.definition: To draw a line around; to encircle.
To limit narrowly; to restrict.
senses.example: The new regulations circumscribe the authority of local inspectors, preventing them from issuing fines directly.

core.definition: In geometry, to draw a shape around another so that its boundary passes through every vertex of the inner shape.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SUR, and the middle syllables are reduced to 'kum'. The final b is pronounced, so the word ends in a clear 'skryb', not a soft 'skry'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in geometry. In everyday or policy use it can sound restrictive, since it suggests limiting someone's freedom.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, circumscribe is mostly formal or written; people more often say limit or restrict. Outside math, it appears in legal, policy, and academic writing, as in circumscribe someone's authority. In geometry, the term is always circumscribe, and the opposite operation is inscribe.

distinctions.note: Inscribe means drawing a shape inside another so that its vertices touch the outer boundary; circumscribe is the opposite, drawing the outer shape around the inner one.
Limit is a general everyday word; circumscribe suggests drawing a clear boundary around something, often in a formal way.
Restrict focuses on reducing freedom or access; circumscribe emphasizes setting a boundary, often in a formal or legal context.

collocations: circumscribe the powers of the office
circumscribe the scope of the project

examples.everyday: The HOA rules pretty much circumscribe what you can do with your front yard.
examples.professional: Let's circumscribe the scope of this sprint so we stop adding features every week.
examples.analytical: Kant's critique tries to circumscribe what reason can legitimately know, leaving room for faith outside speculative knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a cookie cutter that marks the outer edge of the dough.
nuance.etymology: From Latin circumscribere 'to draw a line around', from circum 'around' and scribere 'to write, to draw'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with circumcise, which is unrelated in meaning.
Using it to mean describe or write about; it means to draw a boundary or limit something.

senses.definition: A female member of a clan.

core.definition: A female member of a clan, a group of families who trace descent from a common ancestor, especially in Scotland.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on wom. The -woman is pronounced 'WOOM-un', with a short oo like 'book', not a long oh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with a historical or heritage tone, often used in discussions of Scottish families and clan history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'clanswoman' mainly in historical writing, literature, and discussions of Scottish heritage. In everyday talk, people more often say 'clan member' or describe a relative directly, such as 'she's from our clan'. The plural 'clanswomen' is irregular, so use that form rather than adding -s to 'woman' incorrectly.

distinctions.note: A kinswoman is any female relative by blood or marriage; a clanswoman is a member of a clan, which may include people not closely related.
Clan member is a neutral, modern term; clanswoman is more formal, historical and gendered.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a proud clanswoman who could name every branch of our family tree.
examples.professional: The guide explained how a clanswoman's role in the household was tied to the clan's land and its survival.
examples.analytical: In many Highland accounts the clanswoman appears only in the margins, yet her labor sustained the clan's economy and its households.

nuance.analogy: Like a keeper of the family photo album who knows every name and story, a clanswoman carries the memory and bonds of her whole family line.
nuance.etymology: From clan, from Scottish Gaelic clann, meaning children or offspring, with the noun woman.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'woman' with a long o, as in 'WOH-man', instead of the short oo sound.
Forming the plural as 'clanswomans'; the correct plural is 'clanswomen'.

senses.definition: Having an obstructed flow; blocked.
senses.example: the toilet is clogged

core.definition: Blocked or obstructed, so that liquid, air or something else cannot move freely through a pipe, filter, nose or passage.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, so the -ed is simply a final d sound after the g. Do not add a vowel, and do not pronounce the g as a j sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, because it describes a problem. It can also be used for a head cold or stuffy sinuses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'clogged' for drains, pipes, filters, arteries, and sinuses. In everyday talk, 'my nose is clogged' or 'the drain's clogged' is very natural. Use 'stuffy' when a room feels hot and stale, and use 'clogged' for things that are physically blocked. A common reply is 'Try some hot water and dish soap first.'

distinctions.note: Blocked is more general and can describe a road or a view, while clogged suggests debris or buildup inside a pipe, filter, or passage.
Stuffy describes a stale room or a nose that feels congested, while clogged describes something physically obstructed.

examples.everyday: The kitchen sink is clogged again, so we need to buy a drain snake this weekend.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows a clogged queue, so we need to find out which job is holding up the batch.
examples.analytical: A clogged system does not fail all at once; the blockages accumulate until small changes produce disproportionate delays.

nuance.analogy: Like a straw full of wet leaves, where liquid can still push through only very slowly.
nuance.etymology: From clog, a block or lump, of uncertain origin, plus the past participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g as in 'jog' or adding a syllable, as in KLAW-ged.
Using clogged for a stuffy room, where stuffy is more natural in American English.

conversation.text: The kitchen sink is clogged again.
My nose is so clogged I can't smell anything.
The toilet's clogged, so use the other bathroom.

senses.definition: A temporary group or union of organizations, usually formed for a particular advantage.
senses.example: The Liberal Democrats and Conservative parties formed a coalition government in 2010.

senses.definition: (rare) A group of cheetahs.
senses.example: We spotted a coalition of five cheetahs resting in the shade on the savanna.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A temporary alliance of separate groups, parties, or nations, formed to achieve a shared goal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'LISH', the third syllable. The first and last syllables are light, with a reduced 'uh'; don't stress the first syllable or pronounce the 'i' as a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a practical partnership, though critics may call it an unstable or unlikely union.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'coalition' most often in politics and news ('a coalition government', 'a coalition of civil rights groups'), and sometimes for any temporary group working on one issue. It is more formal than 'team' or 'group' and is not used for a casual circle of friends. The rare sense 'a group of cheetahs' appears only in nature writing.

distinctions.note: An alliance is usually a more formal, longer-lasting agreement between nations or organizations; a coalition is often temporary and built around a specific goal.
A bloc is a larger, more lasting group of countries or parties with shared interests; a coalition may be brief and practical.
A faction is a dissenting subgroup within a larger organization; a coalition is a union of separate groups.

examples.everyday: My neighbors formed a coalition to stop the city from widening our street.
examples.professional: Our data privacy coalition of six companies is publishing shared standards this quarter.
examples.analytical: A coalition differs from a party because its members share a goal rather than a full ideology, which makes it fragile.

nuance.analogy: A coalition is like a carpool: different people with different destinations sharing one ride for a single trip.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin 'coalitio', from Latin 'coalescere', to unite; it is related to 'coalesce'.
common_mistakes: Using 'coalition' for any small team; it implies separate groups that have come together, usually for a political or social goal.
Confusing it with 'coalescence', which means the act or process of merging.

coalition.etymology: Middle French *coalition*, from Medieval Latin *coalitiō*, from Latin *coalitus*.

senses.definition: To put together (something) without adequate preparation or equipment; to improvise (something) minimally usable.
senses.example: We had no proper tools, so we cobbled together a shelf from scrap wood and two old bricks.

core.definition: To put something together quickly from whatever materials are available, producing a rough but usable result.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'geth' in 'together', and 'cobble' has a light secondary stress. The second syllable of 'cobble' and the first syllable of 'together' are reduced, and the 't' in 'together' is a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it suggests improvising under pressure and a lack of polish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cobble together' for quick fixes like dinner from leftovers, a presentation made the night before, or a team put together on short notice. It is often said with a shrug or mild apology. A natural reply to someone who did it well is 'Nice work, given the short notice.'

distinctions.note: 'Throw together' suggests doing something very quickly and possibly carelessly, while 'cobble together' implies using scraps to make something functional.
'Improvise' means creating something on the spot without preparation, while 'cobble together' can happen after some planning, just with limited resources.

examples.everyday: I didn't have time to shop, so I cobbled together a sandwich from what was in the fridge.
examples.professional: We cobbled together a temporary dashboard for the board meeting, but the data pipeline still needs a proper rebuild.
examples.analytical: Many institutions are cobbled together from older rules, so their present form reflects accident more than design.

nuance.analogy: Cobbling together is like patching a leaky boat with whatever wood and rope you can find, so it floats long enough to reach shore.
nuance.etymology: From 'cobble,' meaning to mend roughly, as a shoemaker might, related to 'cobbler.'
common_mistakes: Using a different preposition, such as 'cobble up' or 'cobble with'.
Pronouncing 'cobble' with a long 'o' as in 'cove' instead of 'KAH'.
Saying 'cobble together' with no stress shift, which makes the phrase sound flat.

senses.definition: A proud or conceited person.

core.definition: A proud, conceited person who acts like the most important or dominant person in a group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first word cock and on walk, with of and the reduced to weak sounds. Say it as one smooth phrase, with uv and thuh barely heard.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes someone who is full of themselves, often with a hint of mockery.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom for someone who struts around as if he or she is the biggest shot in a group, such as a team, office or neighborhood. It is informal and is usually said about a person rather than to them, because it insults their ego. A natural reply is 'Yeah, he's been strutting since the promotion' or simply 'Ha, true.'

distinctions.note: A big shot is someone important or influential, which can be neutral; cock of the walk stresses a swaggering ego and is clearly critical.
A show-off performs to get attention, often briefly; cock of the walk describes a settled attitude of dominance over others.

collocations: strut around like the cock of the walk
think he's the cock of the walk
the cock of the walk in the office
be the cock of the walk

examples.everyday: Ever since he won the bowling league, Mike has been strutting around like the cock of the walk.
examples.professional: Dana acted like the cock of the walk in the planning meeting, shutting down every idea except her own.
examples.analytical: In a hierarchy built on rivalry, the man who sees himself as the cock of the walk is often the one most afraid of losing his place.

nuance.analogy: Like the boss rooster in a barnyard, who crows louder than all the others to prove he still rules the yard.
nuance.etymology: Cock (rooster) plus the walk, meaning the dominant bird of a farmyard.
common_mistakes: Using it as a compliment; the idiom is almost always negative.
Saying 'king of the walk', which is not the fixed idiom.

senses.definition: Ordinary; not having any remarkable characteristics.
senses.example: The commonplace sight of traffic jams no longer surprised anyone in our crowded city.

senses.definition: A platitude or cliché.
senses.example: His sermon was full of commonplaces about faith that everyone had heard before.

senses.definition: Something that is ordinary; something commonly done or occurring.
senses.example: Losing a set of keys is a commonplace in our busy household.

senses.definition: A memorandum; something to be frequently consulted or referred to.
senses.example: The lawyer's commonplace of statutes sat open on her desk all day.

senses.definition: A commonplace book.
senses.example: In college, she filled a commonplace book with quotes from Augustine and Emily Dickinson.

senses.definition: To make a commonplace book.
senses.example: I commonplace the most striking passages from each book I read.

senses.definition: To enter in a commonplace book, or to reduce to general heads.
senses.example: She commonplaced every striking quotation from her sermons into a notebook for later use.

core.definition: Ordinary and not special or surprising, something that happens or is seen often.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, KAH, and the second syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'KAH-mun,' not 'KOM-on.' The final syllable rhymes with 'face.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It suggests something ordinary, sometimes dull, but not necessarily bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use commonplace in written reports, editorials, and polished speech, often to say something is no longer surprising, such as 'Remote work is commonplace now.' In casual talk, people tend to say 'everyday' or 'normal.' A natural reply might be 'Yeah, it's pretty commonplace these days.'

distinctions.note: Common is the broad, everyday word for frequent or shared; commonplace is a slightly more formal adjective emphasizing that something is ordinary and unremarkable.
Ordinary means not special, while commonplace emphasizes that something happens so often that it no longer attracts attention.

examples.everyday: Video calls are pretty commonplace now, so nobody thinks twice about them.
examples.professional: Automated testing has become commonplace on our team, so it is part of every release.
examples.analytical: What seems commonplace today was once a contested innovation, and its ordinariness conceals its historical significance.

nuance.analogy: A commonplace object is like a coffee mug in a kitchen: you use it every day and never think about it.
nuance.etymology: From common plus place, originally a 'place' in a book for a common topic, later meaning an ordinary idea.
common_mistakes: Using commonplace to mean 'widespread but praiseworthy'; the word often suggests dullness.
Confusing the noun 'commonplace' (a cliché) with the adjective meaning ordinary.

commonplace.etymology: A Latin *locus commūnis*, referring to a generally applicable literary passage, itself a calque of Ancient Greek *κοινὸς τόπος*.

senses.definition: To be in battle or in a rivalry with another for the same thing, position, or reward; to contend.
To be in a position in which it is possible to win or triumph.
To take part in a contest, game or similar event.
To strive to achieve or obtain something which another also strives for, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

core.definition: To try to win or gain something that others are also trying to get, such as a prize, a job, or customers.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, which is a long 'ee' sound. The first syllable is a weak 'kum', not 'com' or 'cahm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes healthy effort, but can sound harsh when the context is cutthroat or personal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use compete constantly in school, sports, business, and job searches. You compete for something (a prize, a job, a customer) or compete with or against someone. In casual talk, 'Are you competing?' usually means entering a contest or race.

distinctions.note: Contend is more formal and can mean struggling against difficulties or arguing a point, while compete is about rivalry for the same reward.
Vie suggests eager striving for a position or favor and is more literary, while compete is the everyday word.
Rival is a noun or verb for a person or group you are against, often with personal history, while compete describes the act of trying to win.

examples.everyday: My son is competing in the spelling bee next Saturday.
examples.professional: We need to know which competitors are going after the same enterprise customers, because we may have to compete on price.
examples.analytical: Marx's account of class struggle assumes that workers and capitalists compete for a share of the same surplus value.

nuance.analogy: Like runners lining up for the same finish line, each person competes by trying to reach the prize first.
nuance.etymology: From Latin competere, 'to strive together' or 'come together.'
common_mistakes: Using 'compete to' with a person as the object; say 'compete with' or 'compete against' a person, and 'compete for' a prize or job.
Mispronouncing it as 'COM-pete' with stress on the first syllable; the stress belongs on the second syllable.

compete.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *competer*, from Latin *competō* (“to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of”), from *com-* (“with”) + *petō* (“to seek; to aim for, strive for”).

senses.definition: Uncritically satisfied with oneself or one's achievements; smug.
senses.example: He grew complacent as the years rolled on and the money rolled in.

senses.definition: Unduly unworried or apathetic with regard to a need or problem.
senses.example: He tried to paint his audience as complacent, yelling that if they weren't mad as hell then they weren't paying enough attention.

core.definition: Pleased with yourself or your situation so much that you stop trying to improve or stop noticing problems.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PLAY. The final -ent is a reduced, unstressed syllable, so do not say it as a strong 'ent' like 'went'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests smugness or dangerous overconfidence, and Americans use it to criticize people or companies that stop working hard or ignore risks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use complacent in workplace and political talk, for example 'We can't get complacent now that we're ahead.' It is more formal than 'too comfortable,' but common in news and business writing. Saying someone is complacent is a real criticism, so use it carefully about a friend or colleague.

distinctions.note: Content means peacefully satisfied with what you have, usually with no negative judgment. Complacent implies you should be doing more or watching for danger.
Complaisant means eager to please others, not satisfied with yourself. The two words look alike but mean very different things.

examples.everyday: My brother got really complacent after he got the promotion, and now he barely studies for anything.
examples.professional: We can't get complacent about the model's accuracy just because last quarter's numbers looked good.
examples.analytical: Complacent acceptance of the status quo can conceal moral failure, since satisfaction blinds us to injustice we have stopped looking for.

nuance.analogy: A goalie who thinks the game is already won and stops watching the ball.
nuance.etymology: From Latin complacere, to be very pleasing to, from com- (intensive) and placere, to please.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with complaisant, which means eager to please others.
Using it as a neutral word for 'calm'; it usually carries a criticism.

complacent.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *complacēns* (“very pleasing”), present participle of *complacēre* (“to please at the same time, be very pleasing”), from *com-* (“together”) + *placēre* (“to please”); see *please* and compare *complaisant*.

senses.definition: Way to combine simple objects or data types into more complex ones.
The act of putting together; assembly.
senses.example: The composition of the workshop's new furniture took the team three full days.

senses.definition: A mixture or compound; the result of composing.
senses.example: The resulting composition of the paint was thick and slightly sticky.

senses.definition: The proportion of different parts to make a whole.
senses.example: The recipe's composition calls for two parts flour to one part butter.

senses.definition: The general makeup of a thing or person.
senses.example: Her calm composition made her the perfect candidate for the crisis team.

senses.definition: An agreement or compromise by which a creditor or group of creditors accepts partial payment from a debtor.
senses.example: The creditors accepted a composition of forty cents on the dollar to settle the debts.

senses.definition: An essay.
senses.example: For her English class, she wrote a composition about her grandmother's immigration story.

senses.definition: The formation of compound words from separate words.
senses.example: Word composition in German often joins several nouns into one long term.

senses.definition: A work of music, literature or art.
senses.example: The orchestra performed a new composition by a young Brazilian pianist.

senses.definition: Applying a function to the result of another.
senses.example: In the lecture, the professor showed how composition of two functions yields a new function.

senses.definition: Synthesis as opposed to analysis.
senses.example: Her philosophy paper emphasized composition over analysis, building new ideas from existing theories.

senses.definition: The arrangement and flow of elements in a picture.
senses.example: The photographer's composition placed the lighthouse on the left third of the frame.

senses.definition: The characters, roles, weapons, etc. being used by a team.
senses.example: team composition

senses.definition: A puzzle created by the composer using chess pieces on a chessboard, which presents the solver with a particular task.
senses.example: The chess composition required White to mate in three moves despite Black's strong defense.

senses.definition: Typesetting.
The compounding of two velocities or forces into a single equivalent velocity or force.
senses.example: Using vector composition, the pilot calculated the plane's resultant velocity in the crosswind.

core.definition: The combining of simpler objects or data types to form a more complex one, so that the whole is built from its parts.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'ZIH,' the third-from-last syllable area, and the ending is pronounced 'shun,' not 'tee-on.' Reduce the 'puh' in the middle to a quick schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a design or structural relationship with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In software, Americans say 'composition over inheritance' as a common design principle. In everyday life, 'composition' usually means a piece of music, writing or art, or a school essay. Context tells you which sense is meant.

distinctions.note: Composition is the act or structure of combining; composite is the resulting combined thing, or the adjective describing it.
Aggregation groups items loosely, with each part able to exist independently. Composition implies a stronger whole-part relationship, where the parts depend on the whole.

examples.everyday: Her composition of the family photo was great, since everyone was in the frame.
examples.professional: We're using composition instead of inheritance so each class is built from smaller, reusable parts.
examples.analytical: Composition of functions is associative, which lets us build complex pipelines from simple transformations.

nuance.analogy: Like making a sandwich from separate ingredients rather than buying a pre-made one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin compositio, from componere 'to put together.'
common_mistakes: Using 'composition' to mean calmness, which is 'composure.'
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'kom-puh-ZISH-un,' which sounds unnatural.

composition.etymology: From Middle English *composicioun*, borrowed from Old French *composicion*, from Latin *compositiō*.

senses.definition: Able to be comprehended.

core.definition: Able to be understood or grasped by the mind, so that the meaning is clear enough to follow.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'HEN.' The final '-ible' is reduced to 'ih-bul,' and the 'r' in 'pruh' should be clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes clarity of meaning and is often used as praise for explanations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'understandable' or 'easy to follow' in casual speech. 'Comprehensible' sounds more formal or academic and appears in education and language teaching, as in 'comprehensible input.' Use it for ideas, messages and explanations rather than for people.

distinctions.note: Understandable is everyday and common in speech. Comprehensible is more formal and often used for complex material.
Comprehensive means covering everything or including all parts. It has no meaning of clarity, so don't confuse the two.

examples.everyday: Honestly, your explanation was comprehensible, even if the math went over my head.
examples.professional: Please make the dashboard comprehensible to non-technical stakeholders by removing the jargon.
examples.analytical: A theory is not comprehensible merely because its terms are familiar; its logic must be traceable from premise to conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a road map: it is useful only if you can read its symbols and follow its routes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin comprehensibilis, from comprehendere 'to seize together, grasp.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'comprehensive,' which means complete rather than clear.
Stressing the wrong syllable, or dropping the 'r' in 'pruh.'

senses.definition: Agreement; concurring.
An instance of simultaneous occurrence.
senses.example: The concurrence of the two storms flooded the valley faster than anyone predicted.

core.definition: Agreement with an opinion, decision, or plan; also an instance of two things happening at the same time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUR, and the final -ence is a reduced 'uhns.' Keep the r strong, as in American 'concur,' and avoid turning the ending into 'ence' as in 'hence.'

nuance.connotation: Positive to neutral. It signals considered agreement, often by an authority or group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use concurrence in formal writing, legal and government contexts, and business approvals, as in 'with the concurrence of the board.' In casual speech they say 'agreement' or 'everyone's on board.' Do not confuse it with 'concurrency' in technical settings.

distinctions.note: Agreement is everyday and general; concurrence is formal and often implies an official or considered endorsement.
Coincidence is an accidental occurrence of events; concurrence is either formal agreement or a planned simultaneous occurrence.

examples.everyday: We did it with the concurrence of the whole family, so nobody felt left out.
examples.professional: The change needs concurrence from the security team before we can deploy it.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a concurrence of independent sources, not on a single authority.

nuance.analogy: Concurrence is like a group of people raising their hands together after the same vote.
nuance.etymology: From concur, from Latin concurrere, 'to run together,' with the noun ending -ence.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'concurrency,' the computing term
Spelling it with one r
Using it in casual speech where 'agreement' is more natural

senses.definition: A range defined such that there is a fixed probability that the value of the measured parameter will fall within the range.
senses.example: The poll reported 52 percent support, with a confidence interval of plus or minus three points.

core.definition: A range of values, calculated from sample data, that has a set probability of containing the true value of a population parameter.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on IN in interval, with secondary stress on the first syllable of confidence. The middle syllables of confidence reduce to a schwa, so it is kon-fuh-dens, not kon-fi-DENCE. The ər in interval is an American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confidence interval in statistics, data science, research reports, and business analytics, often shortened to CI in tables and slides. People outside technical fields may hear it in news about polls, where it appears as the margin of error.
