senses.definition: A pre-arranged time when a person whose occupation frequently takes them away from their office during working hours is available in their office to answer questions or provide assistance without the requirement for an appointment.
senses.example: If you need help with the homework, the professor will be holding office hours on Thursday from 7–9pm.

core.definition: The regular weekday hours, typically about 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., when an office is open and staffed; also a set time a professor or adviser is available to meet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OF in 'office' and give 'hours' a lighter secondary stress. The h in hours is silent, so say it as 'ow-erz'. In fast speech the two words link: 'AW-fi-SOW-erz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a practical, factual term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use office hours for the workday of an office, as in 'the bank's office hours,' but for shops and banks they often say 'business hours.' In universities, office hours are a set time when a professor is available for students without an appointment, and students often say 'I'm going to office hours.' Always use the plural: 'office hours,' not 'office hour.'

distinctions.note: Business hours describe when a shop, bank or company serves the public; office hours describe when staff are at their desks or available to meet.
Working hours is a general term for the time spent at a job; office hours specifies the schedule of an office or an advisor's availability.
After hours means outside normal opening or working times; office hours refers to the regular, scheduled times when people are present.

examples.everyday: The passport office is only open during regular office hours, so go early in the morning.
examples.professional: Office hours for the data team are Tuesday from 2 to 3, if you want to walk through the model.
examples.analytical: The phrase carries an implicit promise: a professor's office hours offer students equal access to teaching outside the lecture hall.

nuance.analogy: Office hours are like a public counter in a library: the door is open at set times, so anyone can come in with a question.
nuance.etymology: Office comes from Latin officium 'duty, service'; hours comes from Old English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'office hour' in the singular; the phrase is almost always plural.
Pronouncing the h in hours; the word is said as 'ow-erz'.

senses.definition: Endorsement; approval; acceptance; acquiescence.
senses.example: We can start as soon as we get the OK.

senses.definition: To approve; to accept; to acquiesce to.
senses.example: I don't want to OK this amount of money.

senses.definition: To confirm by activating a button marked OK.
senses.example: Please OK the changes on the screen before you close the window.

senses.definition: All right, acceptable, permitted.
senses.example: Is it OK if I spend the night?

senses.definition: Satisfactory, reasonably good; not exceptional.
senses.example: The soup was OK, but the dessert was excellent.

senses.definition: Satisfied (with); willing to accept a state of affairs.
senses.example: I'm OK with the schedule change, as long as we finish by Friday.

senses.definition: In good health or a good emotional state.
senses.example: He's not feeling well now, but he should be OK after some rest.

senses.definition: Satisfactorily, sufficiently well.
senses.example: The team did OK in the playoffs.

senses.definition: Used to indicate acknowledgement or acceptance.
senses.example: I promise to give it back. – OK.

senses.definition: Used to dismiss a dialog box or confirm a prompt.
senses.example: The popup read 'Changes saved' and I just muttered 'OK' and closed it.

senses.definition: Used to introduce a sentence in order to draw attention to the importance of what is being said.
senses.example: OK, I'm thinking of a number…

senses.definition: Used in turn-taking, serving as a request to the speaker to grant the turn to the interrupter.
senses.example: You always do this to me! When we were at your mother’s, you said that… – OK, OK, …

senses.definition: Used to sarcastically or sardonically indicate agreement with the previous statement.
senses.example: You forgot the report again? OK, great, that's exactly what the boss needed.

core.definition: All right; acceptable or satisfactory. Often used as an interjection to agree, confirm or move on.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'kay', and keep the first syllable as a reduced 'uh'. Spell it OK in writing, though it is pronounced as one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals acceptance or agreement, though 'OK' alone can sound lukewarm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use OK constantly, in speech and in email, even at work, as agreement, a check-in or a closing word. Both OK and okay are accepted, with OK more common in writing. In a formal report, prefer acceptable or satisfactory, and avoid OK when you mean excellent.

distinctions.note: Fine can mean all right or good and is a more neutral choice in casual speech, while OK focuses on acceptability.
Acceptable is formal and precise, meaning it meets a standard, while OK is informal.
Alright is an informal spelling discouraged in formal writing; OK or all right is preferred.

examples.everyday: Is it OK if I bring my cousin to dinner on Saturday?
examples.professional: The revised timeline looks OK to me, so I'll send it to the client today.
examples.analytical: The argument works in the easy cases, but it is only OK as a sketch, not yet a proof.

nuance.analogy: Like a green light at a traffic signal: it says go without claiming this is the best route.
nuance.etymology: Disputed origin; popularized in 1839 American newspapers, possibly from a joke abbreviation of 'oll korrect'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'okey' when you mean the everyday word OK; okey is a Turkish tile game.
Using OK to mean excellent in formal writing, where satisfactory or good is more precise.

senses.definition: Something which portends or is perceived to portend either a good or evil event or circumstance in the future, or which causes a foreboding; a portent or augury.
senses.example: The ghost's appearance was an ill omen.

senses.definition: A thing of prophetic significance.
senses.example: A sign of ill omen.

senses.definition: To be an omen of.
senses.example: The sudden drop in sales may omen a difficult year for the small bakery.

senses.definition: To divine or predict from omens.
senses.example: The ancient priests would omen the future by studying the flight of birds.

core.definition: A sign that is believed to predict a good or bad event in the future.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, OH. The second syllable is a reduced 'mun', not 'men'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in form, but often negative when people say 'a bad omen'. Speakers use it half-jokingly in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'bad omen' or 'good omen' when something minor happens and they want to comment on it, like a flat tire before a big event. A natural reply is 'Let's hope not', or 'Don't worry, it's just a coincidence'. In formal writing, the word can also mean a sign of what is coming in politics, the economy, or history.

distinctions.note: A sign is any indication of something, while an omen is a sign of a future event, often one that seems supernatural or significant.
A portent is more formal and literary, and it suggests a dramatic or frightening future event, while an omen can be small or casual.

examples.everyday: A black cat crossed my path this morning, and my grandmother would have called that a bad omen.
examples.professional: Two missed deadlines in one week may be an omen that our project plan needs a serious rebuild.
examples.analytical: Roman priests read the flight of birds as omens, interpreting divine approval or displeasure from the natural world.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather vane that does not control the wind but shows which way it is blowing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin omen, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'men' rather than the reduced 'mun'.
Confusing omen with ominous: the noun is omen, and the adjective is ominous, as in an ominous sign.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, the word for sign is 'ot, and in Greek it is sēmeion, both used for signs and indications. Genesis 1:14 says the lights in the sky are to be for signs and for seasons, presenting the heavens as a God-given source of meaning. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 forbids Israel from seeking omens through divination and similar practices. Genesis 44:5 describes Joseph's silver cup being used in a supposed act of divination, which the story treats as part of a test rather than genuine insight.

senses.definition: In a queue; waiting one's turn for something.
senses.example: I'm waiting on line at the bakery.

core.definition: Waiting in a queue or line, usually in a row with others, for one's turn to be served or to get something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LINE, and 'on' is weak and reduced. Make the diphthong in 'line' clear, moving from ah to ee, rather than a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical situation and is usually neither positive nor negative.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans say 'in line' for waiting in a queue, and 'on line' is used mainly in some regions, especially the New York area, or in informal speech. People also say 'on line' to mean 'connected to the internet,' so context matters. A natural reply is 'How long is the wait?' or 'Got it, I'll get in line.'

distinctions.note: In line is the standard American phrase for waiting in a queue; on line is common in some regions and informal speech.
Online means connected to the internet, a different sense from waiting in a queue; in a virtual setting, Americans write 'online' as one word.
In queue is mainly used in computing or technical contexts for tasks waiting to be processed; Americans say 'in line' for people.

examples.everyday: We waited on line for an hour at the bagel shop this morning.
examples.professional: Your ticket is still on line behind two others in the support queue, so expect a short delay.
examples.analytical: A theory of justice must explain why people on line for scarce goods accept waiting rather than seizing them.

nuance.analogy: Like people waiting at a deli counter, each one moving forward when the person ahead is served.
nuance.etymology: From line, from Latin linea, 'linen thread,' through Old French; the waiting sense comes from people standing in a row.
common_mistakes: Using 'on line' in most of the US where Americans say 'in line'.
Confusing 'on line' for waiting with 'online' for internet access.

senses.definition: Synonym of on site.
senses.example: filmed on location [collocation in movie credits]

core.definition: At the actual place where work, filming or an event is happening, rather than in a studio or office.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -KAY- in 'location', the third syllable, and the final syllable is a weak 'shun'. In fast speech 'on' becomes a weak 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical arrangement without strong emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'on location' mainly in film, television, photography and journalism, for shoots or reports held outside a studio. For work at a client's building or a facility, business speakers usually say 'on site' instead. A natural reply is 'Where are you shooting?' or 'Oh, that sounds exciting.'

distinctions.note: On site is the common business term for work at a particular facility; on location is usually used for filming, field research or events.
Off site means away from the main building or place, often for meetings or training, and is usually the opposite of on site.
In studio means in a controlled indoor production space, while on location means outside it in a real setting.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a sound engineer, and he's on location in Utah this week for a nature documentary.
examples.professional: The marketing team shot the product photos on location at the brewery to show the real process.
examples.analytical: Ethnographers insist that fieldwork conducted on location shapes what researchers are able to observe at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a reporter standing at the scene instead of summarizing the story from a desk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin locatio, 'a placing,' from locare, 'to place'.
common_mistakes: Using 'on location' for an office or client site; Americans say 'on site' for that.
Saying 'in location' instead of 'on location'.

senses.definition: Referring to a judgment, decision, or ruling of a court whose decision rests upon the law as it applies to the particular evidence and facts presented in the case.
senses.example: The judge dismissed the appeal on the merits, not because of a procedural error.

core.definition: Judged by the actual facts, arguments, or qualities of the matter itself, not by side issues such as procedure, politics, or who proposed it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAIR, the first syllable of merits, and the middle vowel is weak. The ending is a 'ts' sound, not a 'z' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, because it implies fair judgment based on substance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mainly in legal writing, policy debates, academic argument, and formal business decisions. In legal settings, a ruling 'on the merits' decides the actual claim rather than a technical issue. In meetings, people often say 'Let's judge this on the merits' to set aside personalities.

distinctions.note: Same idea, but 'on its own merits' points to one specific item and is more common in everyday phrasing.
A ruling on procedural grounds avoids the substance of the case, while a ruling on the merits decides the actual claim.

collocations: debate the proposal on the merits
evaluate the case on its merits

examples.everyday: I don't care who suggested it; let's decide on the merits.
examples.professional: Let's evaluate the vendor proposal on the merits, not on who championed it internally.
examples.analytical: A theory of justice should be judged on the merits of its principles rather than on the reputation of its proponents.

nuance.analogy: Like judging a dish by its taste rather than by the fame of the chef.
nuance.etymology: From 'merit,' from Latin 'meritum' (reward, desert), related to 'mereri' (to earn).
common_mistakes: Saying 'by the merits' instead of 'on the merits'.
Thinking 'merits' only means advantages; in this phrase it means the substance of the case itself.

senses.definition: Moving forward.
senses.example: There was an onward rush as the gates opened.

senses.definition: Advanced in a forward direction or toward an end.
senses.example: The onward route follows the river for another twelve miles before reaching the summit.

senses.definition: In a forward direction.
To keep going; to progress or persevere.
senses.example: Despite every setback, she kept onward until her dissertation was finally finished.

senses.definition: To pass (something) onward; to forward.
senses.example: Please onward the invoice to accounting once you've approved it.

core.definition: Moving forward in space or time, away from a starting point and toward the front or a future goal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, so say it as 'werd' with a soft r, not as two separate syllables. Many learners add an extra vowel before the w.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests steady progress and forward movement, and it is often used in motivational or narrative contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'onward' as an adverb in phrases like 'onward and upward' or 'onward to the next step,' often in speeches, sports commentary, or encouraging talk. In everyday speech Americans more often say 'forward' or 'ahead,' so 'onward' can sound a little formal or dramatic. As an adjective, it is less common and usually appears in set phrases.

distinctions.note: Forward is the everyday word for moving toward the front, while onward often implies continued progress toward a goal.
Ahead refers to a position in front of someone, whereas onward stresses continued motion along a path.

examples.everyday: After we got the car fixed, we drove onward toward the coast.
examples.professional: Once the pilot passes review, we will move onward to the full rollout next quarter.
examples.analytical: The argument moves onward from premise to conclusion, but it never justifies its first assumption.

nuance.analogy: Onward is like a hiker who keeps walking up the trail, never stopping to turn around.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'onweard,' meaning toward, forward, or in front, from 'on' plus '-weard.'
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in 'on-ward-uh.'
Using 'onward' where everyday speech would say 'forward' or 'ahead.'

senses.definition: Able to be operated or used.
Able to be put into operation; practicable.
Able to be treated by surgery.
senses.example: After the scan, the surgeon determined that the tumor was operable and scheduled the procedure.

core.definition: Able to be operated or used, especially a machine or system that works or can be put into working order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AH. The middle syllable is a weak 'per' and the ending -able sounds like 'uh-buhl', not 'ay-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical word with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use operable mostly in engineering, legal, medical and government writing. In everyday speech, they say 'working', 'usable' or 'running'. The more common word in medicine is inoperable, as in 'the tumor was inoperable'.

distinctions.note: Usable means people can use something easily; operable means the system is capable of running or being run.
Operational means currently in service or in use; operable means it is capable of being operated, even if not running now.

examples.everyday: The old truck is still operable, but the heater doesn't work.
examples.professional: The beta release is operable on all three platforms, pending a final security review.
examples.analytical: A theory is operable only if its concepts can be measured against observable outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that not only fits the lock but actually turns it.
nuance.etymology: From operate plus the suffix -able, meaning able to be operated.
common_mistakes: Using operable when you mean operational, which means currently in service.
Stressing the middle syllable, saying 'uh-PER-uh-buhl'.

senses.definition: That opposes or oppose; on the opposite side.
senses.example: opposing armies

core.definition: On the other side of a contest, argument or issue; directly against another party or idea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on POH, the second syllable. The -ing is short, and the first vowel is reduced, so avoid a long first vowel like 'oh-POH-zing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes sides or forces without judging them.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for sides in a game, debate, lawsuit or argument: 'the opposing team', 'opposing counsel'. In everyday speech people often say 'the other team' or 'the other side', and 'opposing' sounds a little formal. It is common in sports reporting and legal talk.

distinctions.note: Opposing describes the other side of a contest or a force against something; opposed describes a person's attitude of disagreement.
Opposite means reversed or facing across; opposing means on the other side of a conflict, not necessarily reversed.

examples.everyday: The opposing team's coach is famous for yelling at the referees.
examples.professional: We should send the proposal to both opposing vendors so the comparison stays fair.
examples.analytical: Hegel argues that every thesis produces its opposing antithesis, and their tension drives history forward.

nuance.analogy: Like two people pulling on opposite ends of a rope in a tug-of-war: both push hard, and neither moves alone.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of oppose, from Latin opponere 'to place against'.
common_mistakes: Using 'opposing' where 'opposite' is meant, as in 'the opposing direction' instead of 'the opposite direction'.
Giving the first syllable a full 'op' vowel; the stress and main vowel are on -POH-.

senses.definition: A person with authority; authority, ordinance.
senses.example: The ordinary's decree required all parishes to hold confession on Saturdays.

senses.definition: A person having immediate jurisdiction in a given case of ecclesiastical law, such as the bishop within a diocese.
senses.example: The diocesan ordinary approved the proposal to close the rural parish.

senses.definition: Something ordinary or regular.
senses.example: Our weekly dinners were the ordinary in an otherwise unpredictable year.

senses.definition: An ordinary person or thing; something commonplace.
senses.example: Sarah's wedding was no ordinary affair, with fireworks over the lake.

senses.definition: A part of the Christian liturgy that is reasonably constant without regard to the date on which the service is performed.
senses.example: The Gloria is an ordinary of the Mass, sung in nearly every service.

senses.definition: A book setting out ordinary or regular conduct.
senses.example: The archdiocese published a new ordinary describing proper conduct for every priest.

senses.definition: A rule, or book of rules, prescribing the order of a liturgy, especially of Mass.
senses.example: The priest checked the ordinary to confirm the readings for Easter Sunday.

senses.definition: A judge with the authority to deal with cases himself or herself rather than by delegation.
senses.example: The ordinary heard the case personally rather than sending it to a delegate.

senses.definition: One of the standard geometric designs placed across the center of a coat of arms, such as a pale or fess.
senses.example: The herald painted a gold chevron ordinary across the center of the shield.

senses.definition: (historical) The chaplain of Newgate prison, who prepared condemned prisoners for death.
senses.example: The ordinary of Newgate visited the condemned men on the night before execution.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A meal provided for a set price at an eating establishment.
senses.example: We ate the ordinary at the tavern for a shilling and a pint.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A penny farthing bicycle.
senses.example: He rode his ordinary down the cobbled lane, wobbling dangerously.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Having regular jurisdiction; now only used in certain phrases.
senses.example: Under canon law, the ordinary authority of the diocese governs these parishes.

senses.definition: Being part of the natural order of things; normal, customary, routine.
senses.example: On an ordinary day I wake up at nine o'clock, work for six hours, and then go to the gym.

senses.definition: Having no special characteristics or function; everyday, common, mundane; often deprecatory.
senses.example: I live a very ordinary life most of the time, but every year I spend a week in Antarctica.

core.definition: Normal, usual and routine; not special, unusual or remarkable in any way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak 'dih,' and the ending '-ary' is pronounced 'air-ee,' so the word has three syllables, not four.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can praise down-to-earth life ('ordinary people') but can also sound dull ('an ordinary restaurant').
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ordinary' often in everyday talk, as in 'just an ordinary day' or 'nothing out of the ordinary.' It can be a compliment when describing hardworking, decent people, but it can sound dismissive when describing a product or experience. 'Mundane' is stronger and more negative, while 'normal' is more neutral.

distinctions.note: Common means shared by many people, while ordinary means having no special qualities; a common problem is widespread, but an ordinary problem is simply unremarkable.
Normal means conforming to an expected standard, while ordinary can suggest plain or unremarkable without any sense of a standard.
Mundane is stronger and more negative, implying boredom or dullness, while ordinary is more neutral.

collocations: in the ordinary course of business

examples.everyday: It was just an ordinary Tuesday, nothing special, so I made pasta and watched a movie.
examples.professional: This is an ordinary bug report, so please assign it to whoever is on call this week.
examples.analytical: Ordinary language philosophers argue that meaning emerges from how words are actually used in everyday contexts.

nuance.analogy: Like plain tap water: useful, everywhere, and nothing special to look at.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ordinarius, 'regular, orderly,' from ordo, 'order.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (or-DIN-ary) instead of AWR-dih-nair-ee.
Using 'ordinary' to mean 'extraordinary' or 'excellent' in a positive sense without context.

ordinary.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *ordenarie*, *ordenaire* et al. Middle French *ordinaire*, and their source, Medieval Latin *ordinarius*, noun use of Latin *ōrdinārius* (“regular, orderly”), from *ordo* (“order”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to orientation.

core.definition: Relating to orientation, meaning direction, position, or a basic stance toward something.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TAY, and the -ation ending is pronounced -AY-shun. The final -al is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'nul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical or academic term that describes a relation to direction or stance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orientational mainly in psychology, sociology, philosophy, and linguistics. In everyday speech, people say 'orientation' as a noun, or use a phrase like 'related to direction.' Avoid using it casually, since it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Orientation is the noun for the state or act of being oriented, while orientational is the adjective that describes something related to it.

examples.everyday: That magazine has a clear political orientation, so it's not really neutral.
examples.professional: The product team needs an orientational review of its goals before we commit to the roadmap.
examples.analytical: Lakoff and Johnson describe orientational metaphors, such as 'happy is up,' which structure everyday thought through spatial relations.

nuance.analogy: An orientational concept is like a compass needle: it does not tell you where to go, but it shows which way you are facing.
nuance.etymology: From orientation, from orient, from Latin oriens, 'rising sun.'
common_mistakes: Using orientational when you need the noun orientation.
Confusing it with orientated, which is less common in American usage.

senses.definition: A mouth or aperture, such as of a tube, pipe, etc. an opening.
senses.example: the orifice of an artery or vein; the orifice of a wound; he entered the cave's gaping orifice

senses.definition: One of the natural external openings of the human or animal body.
senses.example: the vagina and other orifices

senses.definition: A stupid or objectionable person.
senses.example: Don't be such an orifice, Tom; the bus left twenty minutes ago.

core.definition: An opening, such as a mouth, nostril, pipe, or hole, through which something can pass.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ice is pronounced like 'iss', not 'eyes'. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, descriptive word for openings in engineering or anatomy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orifice mainly in technical, medical, or engineering contexts, such as 'the orifice of the valve' or 'the urinary orifice'. In everyday speech they say 'opening', 'hole', or 'mouth' instead. The insulting sense of a stupid person is slang and should be avoided in polite conversation.

distinctions.note: Opening is the everyday, general word, while orifice is precise and used mainly for technical or anatomical openings.
Aperture is used mainly for lens or light openings and is more specialized than orifice.

examples.everyday: The water is coming out of a tiny orifice in the sprinkler, so it probably just needs cleaning.
examples.professional: We need to replace the valve because the orifice has worn and is restricting the flow rate.
examples.analytical: Medical texts describe each natural orifice of the body, from the nostrils to the mouth, as a boundary between inside and outside.

nuance.analogy: An orifice is like the mouth of a bottle, a precise opening through which a liquid must pass.
nuance.etymology: From Latin orificium, from os meaning mouth, and facere meaning to make.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ice as 'eyes'; it is 'iss'.
Using orifice as a casual word for any hole, where opening or hole would sound more natural.

orifice.etymology: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin *ōrificium* (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of *ōs* (“mouth”) + *faciō* (“to make”).

senses.definition: A residential institution for the care and protection of orphans.
senses.example: After her parents died, she grew up in an orphanage on the edge of town.

core.definition: A residential institution that houses, feeds, and cares for children who have no parents or cannot live with them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, OR, and the r is strong. The ph is pronounced as f, and the final -age is pronounced ij, not ayj.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat negative, because it can evoke old-fashioned or institutional care; modern Americans often prefer more positive terms.
nuance.usage_note: Americans still use orphanage, especially for historical institutions or in international contexts, but in the United States child welfare agencies more often use terms like group home, children's home, or residential care. Speaking about a current orphanage in America may sound dated, so use it carefully. In casual talk, people say he grew up in an orphanage to describe a childhood history.

distinctions.note: A foster home is a family household that temporarily cares for a child; an orphanage is an institution.
A group home is a small residential setting for children or adults in need; an orphanage is typically larger and for orphans specifically.

examples.everyday: My coworker volunteers at an orphanage on weekends, teaching the kids to read and play soccer.
examples.professional: Our foundation funds a small orphanage and reports its outcomes to donors each quarter.
examples.analytical: The history of the orphanage in nineteenth-century American cities reveals how charity and social control were intertwined.

nuance.analogy: An orphanage is like a large boarding house that takes in children who have no home to return to.
nuance.etymology: From orphan plus the noun suffix -age, meaning a place or condition; orphan comes from Late Latin orphanus, from Greek orphanos, bereaved.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -age as ayj, as in OR-fuh-nayj.
Dropping the ph sound and saying OR-ta-nij or the like.
Using orphanage for any children's shelter without considering that Americans now often prefer group home or residential care.

senses.definition: To swing back and forth, especially if with a regular rhythm.
senses.example: A pendulum oscillates slower as it gets longer.

senses.definition: To vacillate between conflicting opinions, etc.
senses.example: The mood for change oscillated from day to day.

senses.definition: To vary above and below a mean value.
senses.example: The voltage in the circuit will oscillate around zero at sixty cycles per second.

core.definition: To swing back and forth, often with a regular rhythm; also to keep switching between two opinions, moods or positions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced 'ih' sound, so avoid saying 'oss-il-ate' with a clear 'ill' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, you might hear 'oscillate' about a fan moving side to side, or for a person who keeps changing their mind. Physical meaning is common in product descriptions, such as an oscillating fan. The figurative sense is more formal and slightly literary, so use it for careful description, not casual talk.

distinctions.note: Vacillate focuses on hesitating or wavering in indecision, while oscillate suggests regular back-and-forth movement between two states.
Fluctuate describes irregular rises and falls in quantity or price, while oscillate implies a more regular swinging pattern.

examples.everyday: My brother keeps oscillating between wanting to move to Denver and staying here, so I just let him decide.
examples.professional: The build keeps oscillating between passing and failing, so I think there is a race condition in the test setup.
examples.analytical: Her argument oscillates between a strong claim about divine freedom and a weaker claim about human responsibility, without resolving the tension.

nuance.analogy: A pendulum oscillates, swinging left and right around a center point.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oscillare (to swing), from oscillum (a swing).
common_mistakes: Using the Spanish-like stress oss-i-LATE; the stress is on the first syllable in American English.
Confusing oscillate with oscillation when a noun is needed; say 'the oscillation of the signal'.

oscillate.etymology: Latin *ōscillātus*, perfect passive participle of Latin *ōscillō* (“to swing”) (see *-ate*), from *ōscillum* (“a swing”), usually identified with *ōscillum* (“a little face or mask hung on a tree that sways with the wind”), diminutive of *ōs* (“mouth, face”).

senses.definition: To shine brighter than something else.
To exceed something or someone else, especially in an obvious or flamboyant manner.
senses.example: She managed to outshine every other candidate in the final interview round.

senses.definition: To shine forth, to give out light.
senses.example: At dusk, the lamps along the pier began to outshine the dimming sky.

core.definition: To be so much brighter, better or more impressive than someone or something else that they seem less important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, as in out-SHINE, and use a long i. The past tense outshone is pronounced owt-SHON, with the vowel of 'phone', not 'shined'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for the one who shines, but it can feel unkind if said directly to someone, since it implies the other person was overshadowed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use outshine for people or things that dazzle others: a star player outshining the team, or a kid outshining siblings in a school play. It sounds more vivid than outperform, which is mainly used for business numbers. Saying a junior colleague outshone the boss in a meeting may sound awkward.

distinctions.note: Outperform is a measured business term for doing better on numbers or metrics; outshine is more vivid and about standing out.
Eclipse means to overshadow something so it seems less important, often used for reputations or events; outshine is more about visible brilliance.

examples.everyday: My little brother always manages to outshine me when we sing at family parties.
examples.professional: The new analyst's dashboard completely outshone the old reports in Monday's review.
examples.analytical: Some medieval theologians argued that God's glory outshines every created good, without being diminished by comparison.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch light at noon: the light is still on, but the sun makes it nearly invisible.
nuance.etymology: Compound of out and shine, from Old English scīnan 'to shine'.
common_mistakes: Using outshined as the past tense; the correct form is outshone.
Adding than after outshine; write outshine someone, not outshine than someone.

senses.definition: To transfer the management or day-to-day execution of a business function to a third-party service provider.
senses.example: They decided to outsource the design and manufacture of the system to a vendor.

core.definition: To hire an outside company to perform a business function or service, such as payroll or IT support, instead of doing it in-house.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, SOURCE, with a lighter stress on OUT. The ending is a clear American r in 'sorce', and learners often shorten the vowel or stress the first syllable too heavily.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business settings, but it can sound negative to employees who fear losing their jobs to outside vendors.
nuance.usage_note: Outsource is standard in American business, technology and government contexts. Americans use 'offshore' when work moves to another country, and 'outsource' can mean either domestic or overseas. In casual talk people often say 'hire a company to handle it' instead.

distinctions.note: Offshore specifically means moving work to another country, while outsource only means giving work to an outside party, which can be local.
Subcontract is used when one firm hires another to do part of a contract, often in construction; outsource is broader and common in corporate services.
Delegate means assigning tasks to people inside the organization, while outsource means transferring the function to an external provider.

examples.everyday: My company outsourced its help desk, so now I talk to a team in another state when my laptop breaks.
examples.professional: Let's outsource the regression testing to a vendor so our engineers can focus on the model itself.
examples.analytical: Coase argued that firms exist because internal coordination can cost less than market transactions, and outsourcing reverses that calculation when external markets become cheaper and more reliable.

nuance.analogy: Like hiring a caterer for a party instead of cooking every dish yourself.
nuance.etymology: Formed from out plus source, in the sense of obtaining something from an outside supplier; common in business use from the 1980s.
common_mistakes: Using 'outsource' to mean buying a product; it refers to transferring a business function or process.
Assuming outsource always means overseas work, when Americans often use it for domestic vendors too.

senses.definition: From the interior toward the exterior; in an outward direction.

core.definition: From the inside toward the outside; in an outward direction, away from a center or interior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -wards is reduced to a light 'werdz' with a clear American r. Do not stretch the first vowel into 'ah-oo' or add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes direction or movement and carries no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say outward in everyday speech, as in 'The crack spread outward.' Outwards is correct and understood, but it sounds more British or literary to many US ears. In American writing, outward is the safer default, and outwards appears mainly in formal or literary prose.

distinctions.note: Outward is the standard American form for both adjective and adverb; outwards is a less common adverbial variant with the same meaning.
Outwards describes motion toward the exterior, while outside describes a location beyond a boundary.

examples.everyday: The crowd pushed outwards when the fire alarm went off.
examples.professional: The heat map shows the anomaly spreading outwards from the server cluster in the Virginia region.
examples.analytical: Her ethics begins with the self and moves outwards toward the community, rather than starting with social duty.

nuance.analogy: Like ripples moving from a stone dropped in a pond, something that goes outwards travels from the center toward the edge.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ūtweard, meaning turned toward the outside.
common_mistakes: Using the stressed 'OWT-wards' with a long vowel that sounds like 'out-wards' with a hard ah sound.
Choosing outwards in American business writing where outward is far more natural.

outwards.etymology: From Middle English *outwardes*, from Old English *ūtweardes*; equivalent to *outward* + *s* or *out* + *wards*.

senses.definition: Synonym of over hard.
senses.example: I like my eggs over well, cooked until the yolk is firm all the way through.

core.definition: Of an egg, fried on both sides until the yolk is cooked through and firm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WEL, with a short e as in 'bed,' not a long ay sound. Keep the r in 'over' and do not say 'wail.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical cooking instruction used when ordering food.
nuance.usage_note: 'Over easy,' 'over medium,' and 'over hard' are the usual American diner terms for fried eggs, and 'over well' is a less common variant with the same idea as 'over hard.' If you are not sure a server will understand it, say 'over hard' or 'cooked all the way through.' Diners and breakfast menus are the main setting for this term.

distinctions.note: 'Over easy' means the yolk is still runny, while 'over well' means the yolk is fully cooked and firm.
'Over medium' has a yolk that is set on the outside but still soft in the middle, which is less cooked than 'over well.'

examples.everyday: Can I get two eggs over well with wheat toast, please?
examples.professional: Please note on the catering order that the eggs should be over well, not scrambled.
examples.analytical: Cooking terms like over well show how one preparation can be classified by yolk firmness along a sliding scale.

nuance.analogy: Like a sliding scale from runny to firm: over easy is near one end, and over well is at the firm end.
nuance.etymology: 'Over' from Old English ofer, meaning turned over during frying, and 'well' from Old English wel, meaning fully or thoroughly.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'over well' means 'overcooked'; it means fully cooked through, which is normal for many eggs.
Using 'over well' in a diner when 'over hard' is more widely understood.
Mispronouncing 'well' with a long vowel.

senses.definition: To make excessive commitments, either beyond one's ability or beyond what is reasonable.
senses.example: Don't overcommit yourself this month.

senses.definition: Allocation of more resources than are actually available.
senses.example: The airline's overcommit of seats meant some passengers were bumped at the gate.

core.definition: To promise or take on more tasks, projects, or obligations than you can realistically handle well.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MIT, the same syllable as in commit. The middle syllable 'kuh' is a weak, reduced vowel, so don't pronounce it as a full 'kom'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it implies poor planning or a risk of failure. Americans also use it about themselves with self-deprecating humor, which softens it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overcommit about work, volunteering, and family life, as in 'I think I overcommitted this month.' It comes up often in meetings and at home, usually with a laugh. Natural replies include 'Yeah, I need to learn to say no,' or 'Tell me about it.'

distinctions.note: Overpromise means guaranteeing results you cannot deliver; overcommit means taking on too much, even when each task is reasonable.
Overextend usually concerns stretching your money or resources too thin; overcommit is mainly about time and obligations.
Overbook means selling more seats or appointments than exist, a logistics term; overcommit is about personal or project capacity.

examples.everyday: I said yes to hosting Thanksgiving, baking three pies, and helping my son with his science project, so I've overcommitted myself again.
examples.professional: We overcommitted the sprint by accepting three new features without checking the team's capacity.
examples.analytical: Her argument is that institutions often overcommit to ambitious mission statements they cannot fund, which gradually erodes trust.

nuance.analogy: Like packing a suitcase past the point where the zipper will close: each item seems fine, but the bag won't shut.
nuance.etymology: From over- plus commit, from Latin committere, to bring together or entrust.
common_mistakes: Stressing the verb pattern on the noun: as a noun, overcommitment is pronounced with the stress on the first syllable, OH-ver.
Spelling the past form as overcommited; the correct spelling is overcommitted, with double t.
Using 'overcommit myself' in everyday speech; Americans say 'overcommit yourself' or 'I overcommitted myself'.

senses.definition: To indulge to excess.

core.definition: To enjoy something, such as food, drink, or pleasure, to an excessive degree, often with too much of it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, DULJ, and the first syllables are lighter. The -dulge ends in a soft j sound, like the 'j' in 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests a lack of self-control, though it can be used lightly and humorously.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'overindulge' about food at holidays, desserts, or alcohol, and the tone is usually friendly rather than harsh. You will hear it in phrases like 'I overindulged at Thanksgiving.' A typical reply is 'Me too, I need a walk.' It is a bit more formal than 'eat too much' but still natural in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: 'Overeat' refers only to eating too much food, while 'overindulge' covers food, drink, spending, or any pleasure taken to excess.
'Indulge' can be positive, meaning to treat yourself, while 'overindulge' always implies the amount was too much.

examples.everyday: I overindulged at my sister's birthday party and ate three slices of cake.
examples.professional: Please don't overindulge at the team dinner tonight, because we start the client demo at eight tomorrow.
examples.analytical: Philosophers from Aristotle onward have argued that a virtuous life requires avoiding the tendency to overindulge in pleasure.

nuance.analogy: Overindulging is like filling a glass past the rim: the extra simply spills over.
nuance.etymology: From over (beyond) plus indulge, from Latin indulgere, to be kind to or yield to.
common_mistakes: Using 'on' instead of 'in', as in 'overindulge on dessert', when the standard American phrase is 'overindulge in dessert'.
Putting the stress on the first syllable, which makes the word sound off to American listeners.

senses.definition: To obscure something by casting a shadow.
senses.example: The towering new office building overshadows the small church next door.

senses.definition: To dominate something and make it seem insignificant.
To shelter or protect.
senses.example: The Lord will overshadow you with his wings, and you will find refuge there.

core.definition: To make something seem less important or less noticeable by being much bigger, more impressive or more dramatic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on shad, the second-to-last syllable of the word's main part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on whether the thing overshadowing is positive or harmful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overshadow in news, sports and everyday talk: 'The scandal overshadowed the launch.' It is common and not too formal. It often describes a bigger event making a smaller one feel less important.

distinctions.note: Eclipse suggests a rival outshines someone, often in fame or success, while overshadow more often refers to a thing or event that dominates attention.
Outshine means to be much better than others, while overshadow means to make others seem less important, often by taking attention.

examples.everyday: Don't let your brother's big promotion overshadow your own good news.
examples.professional: The Q3 outage overshadowed the progress we made on the new dashboard.
examples.analytical: Gospel accounts of the transfiguration describe a cloud overshadowing the disciples, which signals God's presence rather than merely darkness.

nuance.analogy: Like a tall building blocking the sun from a small house, making it look dim by comparison.
nuance.etymology: From Old English oferscadian, from ofer (over) and scadian (to shade).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress as oh-ver-SHAD-ow, with an ow diphthong at the end; the final syllable is a light oh.
Using overshadow to mean shade physically in everyday speech; it usually means make something seem less important.
nuance.biblical_note: In Mark 9:7 and Matthew 17:5, a cloud overshadows the disciples at the transfiguration, and in Luke 1:35 the power of the Most High will overshadow Mary. The Greek word episkiazō means to cast a shadow over, suggesting a sheltering or covering presence. In these passages the image signals divine presence and protection rather than something dark.

overshadow.etymology: From Middle English *overschadwen*, *overschadewe*, from Old English *ofersċeadwian* (“to overshadow”), equivalent to *over-* + *shadow*.

senses.definition: Initialism of public address.
Initialism of production assistant.
Initialism of personal assistant.
Initialism of personal appearance.
Initialism of power amplifier.
Initialism of Prince Albert (“genital piercing”).
Initialism of public accountant.
Initialism of public act.
Initialism of physician assistant.
Initialism of physician associate.
Initialism of polyamide.
Initialism of pyrrolizidine alkaloid.
Initialism of Peano arithmetic.
Initialism of pulmonary artery.
Initialism of Parental Accompaniment.
Initialism of precision agriculture.
Initialism of points against.
Initialism of posteroanterior.
Initialism of per annum.
senses.example: an interest rate of 3% PA

core.definition: A public address system, meaning the microphones and speakers used to make announcements in a building, station or stadium.

pronunciation.tip: Say the two letters separately: pee, then AY, with the main stress on the second letter. Do not pronounce it as the word 'pa' or 'pah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell out PA when talking about the sound system in schools, airports, stadiums and stores, as in 'they announced it over the PA.' The abbreviation also means personal assistant in offices and physician assistant in healthcare. Context usually makes the meaning clear, but in a meeting it is worth asking which PA someone means.

distinctions.note: An intercom connects a few specific rooms privately, while a PA broadcasts announcements to a large audience at once.
A speaker is just the device that makes sound, while a PA is the full system of microphones, amplifiers and speakers.

examples.everyday: They announced over the PA that the train was delayed by twenty minutes.
examples.professional: Can you send me the agenda? My PA needs it by noon so she can prepare the meeting room.
examples.analytical: The sound engineer tested the PA before the keynote so that every seat in the hall could hear the speaker clearly.

nuance.analogy: A PA is like a megaphone for a whole building: one voice reaches everyone at the same time.
nuance.etymology: Abbreviation of public address.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the letters as the word 'pa' or 'pah'
Assuming PA always means personal assistant, when it can also mean the sound system or physician assistant
Using PA as a verb in casual speech, where it sounds unnatural

senses.definition: To store away, place out of the way, or stash, especially for the longer term.
senses.example: She packed away her warm sweaters for the summer.

senses.definition: To eat (a great deal of food).
senses.example: Have you ever seen someone pack away five hot dogs in one sitting?

core.definition: To store something in a safe place for later use, often for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on pack, and away carries a secondary stress on the second syllable. In fast speech, the vowel of uh is very weak, so it sounds like pak-uh-WAY.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes ordinary storage or, in informal use, eating large amounts of food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pack away for storing seasonal items, such as winter clothes, or for keeping important things safe. Informally, pack away also means to eat a lot of food quickly, as in he can pack away a whole pizza. It is common in conversation, and the phrase carries a friendly tone.

distinctions.note: Put away is the more general and common phrase for tidying or storing things. Pack away suggests packing items carefully into a container for longer storage.
Store is a neutral, general verb. Pack away is more informal and implies packing something into a box or bag.

examples.everyday: We packed away the winter coats in the closet once spring finally arrived.
examples.professional: We packed away the old prototype data in cold storage before the audit, so it stays accessible but off the main servers.
examples.analytical: Some scholars packed away inconvenient evidence in footnotes, letting the main argument proceed without it.

nuance.analogy: Packing away is like putting a summer wardrobe in a cedar chest until the next season comes around.
nuance.etymology: A phrasal verb formed from pack and away, using the sense of putting things away in a container.
common_mistakes: Saying pack up away, which is wrong; the particle is just away.
Using pack away for putting something on a table; it implies putting it into a container.

senses.definition: To sell or dispose of (something) with the intent to deceive; to attempt to pass off a counterfeit or inferior product as genuine.
senses.example: The seller tried to palm off a fake watch as a genuine vintage Rolex.

core.definition: To sell something inferior or fake to someone by deceiving them into thinking it is genuine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OFF, the particle, so say 'pahm-AWF'. In most US accents 'off' rhymes with 'cough'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies deception or trickery.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use palm off for passing a cheap, defective or fake item on someone, often a used car or a counterfeit product. It is informal and common in everyday talk and news. A typical warning is 'Don't let them palm off a fake on you,' and a natural reply is 'Thanks for the heads-up.'

distinctions.note: Fob off means to put someone off with an excuse or cheap substitute; palm off focuses on selling a bad item as genuine.
Pass off is broader and can refer to passing off yourself or an idea; palm off usually concerns goods or deals.

examples.everyday: The guy at the flea market tried to palm off a cracked phone on me as new.
examples.professional: The vendor tried to palm off an unfinished module as the final release, but our testing caught it.
examples.analytical: Hasty branding can palm off a low-quality product as a premium good, shifting the risk onto the buyer.

nuance.analogy: Like slipping a counterfeit bill into a stack of real money.
common_mistakes: Using palm off without an object; you need something to palm off.
Dropping the 'on' pattern: say palm something off on someone, not palm someone off.

palm-off.etymology: “Palming” an object is a type of sleight of hand, secretly removing the desired article and leaving only the undesired one.

senses.definition: In a way or to an extent that is paradigmatic.
senses.example: The 1960s rebellion stood paradigmatically for the youth movements that followed across Europe.

core.definition: In a way that serves as a clear model, pattern or typical example of something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAT, the fourth syllable. The ending -ically is usually pronounced as 'ih-klee', not 'ih-cal-ly'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term with a slightly formal tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb mainly in academic writing, linguistics and philosophy, and in careful analysis. In casual speech it would sound stiff, so say 'a perfect example of' instead. It is most common in phrases like paradigmatically clear or paradigmatically important.

distinctions.note: Typically describes what usually happens, while paradigmatically means the case serves as an ideal model of the category.
In linguistics, syntagmatically concerns relations within a sequence, while paradigmatically concerns choices that can substitute for one another.

examples.everyday: That diner is paradigmatically American, with its chrome counters and milkshakes.
examples.professional: Our onboarding flow is paradigmatically a case of a form that asks for too much information up front.
examples.analytical: The case is paradigmatically a failure of induction, since the sample is too narrow to support the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a textbook example that makes a rule obvious to everyone who sees it.
nuance.etymology: From paradigm, from Greek paradeigma meaning 'pattern', with the English suffixes -atic and -ally.
common_mistakes: Confusing paradigmatically with paradigm shift; the adverb describes a model example, not a change.
Putting the stress on PAIR instead of on MAT in the middle of the word.

senses.definition: A set that has a given, elsewhere specified partial order.
senses.example: In the lecture, the professor defined a partially ordered set using reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive relations.

senses.definition: The ordered pair comprising a set and its partial order.

core.definition: A set with a partial order, a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, though not every pair of elements needs to be comparable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAHR, OR and SET, one in each word, and ordered is two syllables ending in a plain d sound. In the abbreviation poset, say POH-set with the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians, computer scientists and logicians use it in textbooks and papers, and they often say 'poset,' pronounced POH-set, in conversation. In this sense 'partially' does not mean 'incomplete'; it means that some pairs of elements may be incomparable. Everyday speakers will not use it.

distinctions.note: In a totally ordered set every pair of elements is comparable, so the set forms a single chain; in a partially ordered set some pairs may be incomparable.
A preorder is reflexive and transitive but not necessarily antisymmetric, so two distinct elements can be equivalent to each other.

collocations: Hasse diagram of a partially ordered set
lattice as a partially ordered set

examples.everyday: My husband teaches math, and at dinner he started drawing little diagrams of a partially ordered set on a napkin.
examples.professional: The task dependencies form a partially ordered set, so the scheduler can run unrelated jobs in parallel.
examples.analytical: A partially ordered set need not be a lattice, since two of its elements may have no unique least upper bound.

nuance.analogy: Like a family tree: some relatives are clearly ancestors of others, but two cousins may have no ordering between them.
nuance.etymology: Built from partial (Late Latin partialis, 'of a part'), ordered (Latin ordinare, 'to arrange') and set (Old English settan).
common_mistakes: Assuming partially ordered means only loosely arranged in everyday sense; in math it means some pairs are incomparable
Saying poset with a long o instead of POH-set

senses.definition: The period of time that has already happened, in contrast to the present and the future.
senses.example: a book about a time machine that can transport people back into the past

senses.definition: The past tense.
senses.example: In the sentence, the verb should be in the past, not the present.

senses.definition: Having already happened; in the past; finished.
senses.example: past glories

senses.definition: Following expressions of time to indicate how long ago something happened; ago.
senses.example: Her grandfather left the village fifty years past, and nobody has heard from him since.

senses.definition: Of a period of time: having just gone by; previous. foregone, #:
senses.example: during the past year

senses.definition: Of a tense, expressing action that has already happened or a previously-existing state.
senses.example: past tense

senses.definition: In a direction that passes.
senses.example: I watched him walk past.

senses.definition: Beyond in place or quantity.
senses.example: the room past mine

senses.definition: Any number of minutes after the last hour.
senses.example: What's the time? — It's now quarter past twelve midday (or 12:15 pm). — O.K., we'll stop at half (past) twelve.

senses.definition: No longer capable of.
senses.example: I'm past caring what he thinks of me.

senses.definition: Having recovered or moved on from (a traumatic experience, etc.).
senses.example: After years of therapy, she finally seemed past the accident that had changed her life.

senses.definition: Passing by, especially without stopping or being delayed.
senses.example: Ignore them, we'll play past them.

core.definition: The time that has already happened, before the present moment; everything that occurred before now.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a of 'cat,' not the broad 'pahst' common in British speech. Do not add a vowel after the s-t ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, and it can be warm or wistful when people talk about memories or nostalgia.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use past in everyday talk for time already gone, as in in the past or over the past few years. When telling time, people usually say ten after three in casual speech, though ten past three is understood. As a preposition, past often means beyond, as in it's past due or he walked past the store.

distinctions.note: Passed is the past tense and past participle of the verb pass, as in I passed the store. Past is a noun, adjective, or preposition, not a verb form.
Former refers to a previous role, status, or name, as in my former boss. Past refers to a period of time or events in general.
History is the record of past events studied as a subject, while past is simply the time that has gone by.

examples.everyday: I've lived in Denver for the past five years, and I still miss the ocean.
examples.professional: Our uptime has been above 99.9 percent over the past quarter, which is our best result in two years.
examples.analytical: Historians cannot simply recover the past; they reconstruct it from sources that have already been interpreted by someone.

nuance.analogy: The past is like the rear-view mirror of a car: it shows what you have already passed, and it is useful but not where you are going.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English passed, the past participle of pass, which came to be used as a noun, adjective, and preposition.
common_mistakes: Confusing past with passed, saying I past the store instead of I passed the store.
Using in the past time instead of simply in the past.

past.etymology: From Middle English *passed*, past participle of Middle English *passen* (“to pass, to go by”), whence Modern.

senses.definition: A state of tranquility, quiet, and harmony. For instance, a state free from civil disturbance.
senses.example: Our lounge strives to maintain an environment of peace for the comfort of our customers.

senses.definition: A feeling of tranquility, free from oppressive and unpleasant thoughts and emotions.
senses.example: The safety equipment will give me some peace of mind.

senses.definition: Death.
senses.example: The old king went to his peace in the spring, surrounded by his sons.

senses.definition: Harmony in personal relations.
senses.example: After years of arguing, the two sisters finally found peace in their relationship.

senses.definition: A state free of war, in particular war between different countries.
senses.example: May there be peace in our time.

senses.definition: Peace out; goodbye.
senses.example: Peace, dude, I'm heading out, catch you tomorrow.

senses.definition: To make peace; to put at peace; to be at peace.
senses.example: After the funeral, he finally began to peace with his father's death.

senses.definition: To peace out.
senses.example: I finished my shift, grabbed my bag, and peaced out before my boss noticed.

core.definition: A calm, quiet state without war or fighting, or a calm, untroubled feeling free from stress and worry.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long e and end with a clear s, so it sounds like PEES, not pease or piece. The word has one stressed syllable. Don't confuse it with the homophone piece, which has the same sound but a different meaning.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes calm, harmony, and freedom from conflict or worry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use peace in everyday speech for quiet and calm, as in I just want some peace and quiet, and in news and politics for an end to war. Peace out is informal slang for goodbye, mostly used by younger speakers, and it can sound playful or dated. In a church setting, peace is also a common greeting in the service.

distinctions.note: Piece means a part of something; it is a homophone, so check spelling carefully in writing.
Calm describes a temporary state of being relaxed, while peace suggests a deeper, more lasting harmony.
Quiet refers only to the absence of noise, while peace can mean an inner or social state of harmony.

examples.everyday: I just want a little peace and quiet this weekend after a long week.
examples.professional: Let's call a truce and keep the peace in the meeting so we can finish the migration plan.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes peace as the tranquility of order, a claim that shaped much of Western political thought.

nuance.analogy: Peace is like still water: calm not because nothing moves beneath the surface, but because nothing is churning.
nuance.etymology: From Old French pais, from Latin pax, pacis.
common_mistakes: Confusing peace with piece in writing.
Using in peace with; the usual phrase is at peace with someone or something.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, peace is the Hebrew word shalom, meaning wholeness, completeness, welfare, and right relationship. In the New Testament, the Greek word is eirene, which carries the same sense of harmony restored between God and people. Romans 5:1 says that believers who have been justified by faith have peace with God through Jesus Christ. John 14:27 records Jesus giving his peace to his disciples, distinct from the peace the world gives. Matthew 5:9 says that the peacemakers are blessed, because they will be called sons of God.

peace.etymology: From Middle English *pees*, *pes*, *pais*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *peis* and Old French *pais* (“peace”), from Latin *pāx* (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European **peh₂ḱ-* (“to fasten, stick, place”), related to, see *pact*.

senses.definition: Rush hour.
Relating to peak periods in traffic and transportation.
senses.example: Public transit runs more trains during peak hours, so avoid the platform at five.

core.definition: The busiest times of day, such as morning and evening rush hour, when roads, trains or stores are most crowded.

pronunciation.tip: In American speech, 'hours' carries the main stress and 'peak' is lighter. 'Hours' sounds like 'ow-erz' with a clear r, not like 'ours'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a practical description, sometimes said with a complaint that a time is crowded.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in everyday talk, in transit announcements and at work, often as 'during peak hours' or 'avoid peak hours'. For the morning or evening traffic jam itself, people usually say rush hour. In business, peak hours also means the busiest times for a store, call center or server.

distinctions.note: Rush hour is the specific commute time; peak hours is broader and can cover any busy period, such as lunch at a restaurant.
Off-peak is the opposite: quieter times when crowds or rates are lower.

examples.everyday: Let's leave early so we miss the peak hours on the freeway.
examples.professional: We need extra staff during peak hours, from 11 to 1, at the call center.
examples.analytical: Demand models should separate peak hours from baseline traffic, or the forecast will overstate typical load.

nuance.analogy: Like the high tide of the day's activity, when the water reaches its highest point.
nuance.etymology: Hour comes from Latin hora through Old French; the origin of peak is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Giving both words equal stress; 'hours' is the stronger word.
Using peak hours for a single traffic jam; rush hour is more natural for that.

senses.definition: Characterized by percussion; caused by or related to the action of striking or pounding something.
senses.example: He massaged her shoulders with a gentle percussive action.

senses.definition: Produced by striking organs together, for example, smacking the lips or gnashing the teeth.
senses.example: Linguists describe the sound of smacking lips as a percussive noise, not a spoken vowel.

senses.definition: A percussive phone.
senses.example: In the phonetics lab, the professor classified the click as a percussive.

core.definition: Producing a sharp striking sound, or involving the action of striking or pounding something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUS, the second syllable. The final -ive is a reduced 'iv', not 'eev'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes sound or force and can suggest a sharp, jarring quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'percussive' mostly in music and sound writing, as in 'a percussive guitar style' or 'a percussive attack'. In everyday speech they would say 'clacking' or 'banging'. It is an adjective only, so do not use it as a noun.

distinctions.note: Rhythmic describes a regular, repeating pattern; percussive describes the sharp, striking quality of each sound.
Noisy is general and everyday; percussive is more precise, focusing on sharp impact sounds.

examples.everyday: The dishwasher makes this percussive clatter every time it spins.
examples.professional: The sound engineer added a percussive click to the start of each note so the patch feels more responsive.
examples.analytical: Scholars of early jazz often describe its rhythmic focus as percussive, emphasizing attack over melodic line.

nuance.analogy: A percussive sound is like a single clap, sharp and quick, rather than a long hum.
nuance.etymology: From percussion, with the suffix -ive, from Latin percussus 'struck'.
common_mistakes: Using 'percussive' as a noun; the noun is 'percussion'. The phonetics term 'percussive phone' is technical, not everyday English.
Stressing the last syllable as per-KUS-IV; the stress belongs on KUS.

senses.definition: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.
senses.example: Measure each side and add them up to find the perimeter of the garden.

senses.definition: The length of such a boundary.
The outer limits of an area.
senses.example: circumference.

senses.definition: A fortified strip or boundary usually protecting a military position.
senses.example: Guards patrolled the perimeter after dark, watching for anyone approaching the base.

senses.definition: An instrument for determining the extent and shape of the field of vision.
senses.example: The optometrist used a perimeter to map the patient's peripheral vision loss.

core.definition: The total length of the outside boundary of a shape, or the outer edge of an area.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, RIM, and the last syllable is a reduced er. The middle syllables are weak, so keep them short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise and practical word used in everyday, professional, and security contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perimeter both in math class, where it means the total length around a shape, and in everyday speech about the edge of a yard, a building, or a security zone. You might hear the security team is patrolling the perimeter or the fence marks the perimeter of the property. In math it is used for the length around a shape, while area is the space inside.

distinctions.note: Circumference refers specifically to the boundary of a circle, while perimeter applies to the boundary of any shape.
Border is the general word for an edge between two areas, often political, while perimeter refers to the outer edge of a defined space or shape.

examples.everyday: The kids ran around the perimeter of the backyard, and the dog followed them along the fence.
examples.professional: The security team set up a new perimeter around the data center after the alert.
examples.analytical: To calculate the perimeter, we sum the lengths of the sides, and the formula holds for any polygon whose sides are known.

nuance.analogy: A perimeter is like the outline you trace around a cookie cutter shape: it is the edge you could walk along without stepping inside.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin perimetros, from Greek perimetron, 'a measure around,' from peri, 'around,' and metron, 'measure.'
common_mistakes: Confusing perimeter with area, which measures the inside rather than the boundary.
Stressing the first syllable, as in PER-ih-meter, instead of the second.

senses.definition: To make peripheral; to marginalize.
senses.example: Budget cuts would peripheralize the rural clinics and push their patients toward the city.

core.definition: To push someone or something to the edge of a group or system, making it less important and less involved.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the RIF syllable, not the first one. The ending '-ize' is pronounced 'eyes', so the word ends in 'lyze'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a deliberate choice to reduce someone's influence or role.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'peripheralize' rarely, mostly in policy and academic writing. In everyday speech they say 'marginalize' or 'push to the side'. It is used when the change is structural, such as moving a team out of decision-making.

distinctions.note: 'Marginalize' is the common word for excluding people from influence, often socially. 'Peripheralize' is more structural and often about position in a system.
'Sideline' is informal and suggests taking someone out of play. 'Peripheralize' is more formal and suggests moving them to the edge rather than out entirely.

examples.everyday: I felt like the group chat had peripheralized me after I moved away, so I stopped checking it.
examples.professional: Reorganizing the team risks peripheralizing QA, so we should keep them in the planning meetings.
examples.analytical: Colonial administrations often peripheralized local institutions to concentrate authority in the capital.

nuance.analogy: Like moving a chair from the head of the table to the corner: nobody leaves the room, but the seat no longer matters.
nuance.etymology: From peripheral plus -ize, from Greek periphereia 'circumference'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PER-ih-fuh-ral-ize'.
Confusing the verb with 'peripherally', the adverb.

senses.definition: To pursue in a manner to do harm or cruelty to; especially, because of the victim's race, sexual identity, or adherence to a particular belief.
senses.example: He who persecutes one will persecute all.

senses.definition: To harass with importunity; to pursue with persistent solicitations; to annoy.
senses.example: Our landlord kept persecuting us with calls and letters demanding payment we had already made.

senses.definition: To kill many of one species of animal, with the intent of removing them from human habitats.
senses.example: Humans have been persecuting wolves in this forest for centuries.

core.definition: To treat someone cruelly or unfairly over a long period, especially because of their race, religion or beliefs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PUR. The final syllable is cute, not kyoo-ate, and the middle is a reduced vowel. Learners often add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes serious harm or cruelty and is used in news, history and human rights discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use persecute for serious, sustained mistreatment of a group or person, often because of religion, race or politics. For everyday annoyance they say harass or pester. Using persecute for a small complaint sounds exaggerated, so save it for serious situations.

distinctions.note: Oppress describes ongoing unjust control, often political or economic; persecute emphasizes hostile targeting and harm.
Harass is common and can be used for smaller acts; persecute suggests more severe, systematic cruelty.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's family left their village because they were persecuted for their faith.
examples.professional: The report documents how the regime persecuted journalists who covered the protests.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the early church was persecuted as a group or only in local, intermittent episodes.

nuance.analogy: To persecute is like a relentless storm that does not stop until the house is damaged, rather than a single rainy day.
nuance.etymology: From Latin persequi, to follow closely or pursue, from per- and sequi, to follow.
common_mistakes: Using persecute for everyday annoyance, which sounds dramatic.
Pronouncing the final syllable as kyoot with a long vowel and an extra syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb diōkō means to pursue, chase or harass, and in the New Testament it describes hostile pursuit of believers because of their faith. Matthew 5:10-12 blesses those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake and rejoicing when people revile them. John 15:20 reports Jesus telling the disciples that if they persecuted him they will also persecute them. 1 Timothy 1:13 describes Paul's earlier life as one of persecuting the church, which he later regrets.

persecute.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *persécuter*, from Ecclesiastical Latin *persecutor*, from Latin *persequor* (“follow up, pursue”), from *per* + *sequor* (English *sequel*).

senses.definition: The doctrine that physical objects exist only as perceptual phenomena or sensory stimuli.

core.definition: The philosophical view that physical objects exist only as perceptions or sensory experiences.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'NAH'. The middle syllables are reduced to schwa sounds, and the ending is 'zum', not 'zim'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it names a specific position in the philosophy of perception.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in philosophy classes, academic papers and debates about perception and reality. It is not used in everyday speech. People who discuss it usually explain it with examples like a table existing only as sensations.

distinctions.note: Idealism holds that reality is mental in nature, while phenomenalism claims objects are reducible to actual or possible sensory experiences.
Realism holds that objects exist independently of perception, which phenomenalism denies.

examples.everyday: My roommate is into phenomenalism, so he insists the table only exists when someone is looking at it.
examples.professional: In the reading group, we discussed phenomenalism as one response to skepticism about the external world.
examples.analytical: Berkeley's idealism is often read as a form of phenomenalism, though he would have rejected that label.

nuance.analogy: Phenomenalism is like saying a movie exists only as what we see on the screen, not as a separate thing behind it.
nuance.etymology: From phenomenal (relating to appearances) plus the suffix -ism (doctrine).
