pronunciation.tip: Argument has stress on the first syllable, and the -gu- is quick, so say AR-gyuh-muhnt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical label used in philosophy and theology classes, and it is neither praise nor criticism of the argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in philosophy of religion courses, theology, and debates about intelligent design. It is formal and precise, so use it in academic or serious discussion rather than casual conversation. In everyday talk, people more often say argument from design.

distinctions.note: The ontological argument infers God's existence from the concept of God alone, while the teleological argument infers a designer from observed order in nature.
The cosmological argument reasons from the existence of the universe or its causes, while the teleological argument reasons from the purposeful structure of nature.

examples.everyday: My friend says the beauty of nature proves God made it, which is basically the teleological argument.
examples.professional: In the seminar, our instructor asked us to outline the teleological argument before we discussed its weaknesses.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique of the teleological argument targets the analogy between natural order and human artifacts, questioning whether we can infer a designer from the world's apparent purposiveness.

nuance.analogy: It is like finding a watch on a beach and concluding that someone must have made it, because its parts clearly work together toward a purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Greek telos (end, purpose) and -logical, from logos (reason, study).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in teleological, saying tee-lee-uh-LAH-jih-kuhl with the main stress in the right place but mispronouncing the -gi- sound as a hard g.
Using the term to mean any argument about design, when it specifically refers to an argument for a designer of the universe.

senses.definition: Moderation or self-control in any action; control of the desire to act emotionally; calmness; an instance of this.
(Habitual) moderation in regard to the indulgence of natural appetites and passions; moderate or restrained indulgence.
senses.example: temperance in eating and drinking

senses.definition: Moderation in the use of intoxicating substances; sobriety; specifically, complete abstinence from alcoholic beverages; teetotalism.
senses.example: The church's temperance league pushed for a complete ban on liquor sales.

senses.definition: Synonym of chastity (“abstinence from any sexual activity considered immoral”).
senses.example: Medieval sermons praised temperance as a virtue that guarded the soul from lust.

senses.definition: The action of bringing to a temperate or moderate state.
senses.example: The gradual temperance of the steel makes it less brittle.

senses.definition: Proper moderation between extreme or opposing qualities; an instance of this.
senses.example: Aristotle prized temperance as the mean between indulgence and total denial.

senses.definition: Temperature which is neither too cold nor too hot.
senses.example: Mild temperance in the valley let the orchards bloom weeks early.

senses.definition: (dated) Restraint or self-control when made angry or frustrated; forbearance.
senses.example: Her temperance under insult impressed everyone at the tense meeting.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Advocating or practising complete abstinence from alcoholic beverages.
senses.example: The temperance society held its annual picnic without any alcohol.

core.definition: Moderation and self-control, especially in eating, drinking, and the indulgence of desires and pleasures.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ance ending is reduced to a weak 'uhnts' sound, not a full 'ants'. The first two syllables may blend, so keep the 'p' light.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises self-control and balance, though in American history it is also linked with the temperance movement against alcohol.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use temperance mainly in religious, moral, or historical contexts, and it can sound old-fashioned in casual speech. In the United States, temperance often means abstaining from alcohol because of the nineteenth-century temperance movement. In everyday talk, people usually say moderation or self-control instead.

distinctions.note: Moderation is the everyday term for not overdoing something, while temperance is a more formal moral virtue of self-restraint.
Abstinence means giving something up completely, while temperance can mean balanced use rather than total avoidance, though American usage often narrows it to alcohol.
Self-control is the general everyday term for restraint, while temperance is more formal and often used in discussions of virtue.

examples.everyday: My grandfather believed in temperance, so he never had more than one beer at a barbecue.
examples.professional: Our wellness program encourages temperance with holiday snacks and alcohol at team events, without banning either.
examples.analytical: Aquinas treats temperance as the cardinal virtue that moderates the pleasures of touch and taste, so that appetite serves reason.

nuance.analogy: Temperance is like a good thermostat for the appetites: it keeps the heat of desire at a comfortable level rather than letting it overheat or go cold.
nuance.etymology: From Latin temperantia, meaning moderation or self-restraint, from temperare.
common_mistakes: Using temperance as a general word for cheapness or thrift; it means moderation in indulgence.
Saying a person has a temperance when the natural form is a person of temperance or practices temperance.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea appears as self-control rather than the word temperance in the RSV. The Greek word is enkrateia, meaning self-mastery or control over one's desires. Galatians 5:23 lists self-control among the fruit of the Spirit, which describes restraint over bodily appetites as the work of God in a believer. Acts 24:25 records Paul speaking to Felix about righteousness, self-control, and future judgment, where the same Greek idea is used. 2 Peter 1:6 includes self-control in a list of virtues that believers are to add to their faith.

temperance.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *temperaunce* (“forbearance, restraint; moderation, temperateness; gentleness, modesty; action of achieving a compromise between two extremes; etc.”), from Anglo-Norman *temperaunce*, from Latin *temperantia*…

senses.definition: The act of tempting.
senses.example: The salesman's temptation of the elderly customers led to a complaint with the state.

senses.definition: The condition of being tempted.
Something attractive, tempting or seductive; an inducement, seducement, or enticement.
senses.example: The bakery's free samples were a temptation I could never resist on my morning walk.

senses.definition: Pressure applied to one's thinking designed to create wrong emotions which will eventually lead to wrong actions.
senses.example: Theologians have long debated whether temptation begins in the mind before it becomes action.

core.definition: A strong desire to do something you know you should avoid, or something that attracts you toward it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TAY, and the p is pronounced, not silent. The ending is 'shun', not 'shee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it usually suggests something you should resist, though playful speech can use it for tempting treats, as in 'that cake is a temptation'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say resist temptation or give in to temptation, especially in everyday moral talk and in church. In casual speech they also say a treat is a temptation when they want to eat it. A natural reply to a tempting offer is 'Oh, you're tempting me!'

distinctions.note: An urge is a sudden impulse that is not necessarily wrong. A temptation is attractive precisely because it pulls you toward something you should avoid.
A craving is a strong physical or emotional desire, such as for sweets. Temptation involves a choice between what you want and what you should do.
Allure is the charm or appeal of something, often positive. Temptation implies a pull toward a choice that may be wrong.

examples.everyday: I know I shouldn't, but that donut in the break room is too much of a temptation.
examples.professional: The temptation to ship the feature before testing is strong, so let's add a checklist to the release process.
examples.analytical: Moral philosophy has long asked why the temptation to deceive seems strongest when deception appears to cost nothing.

nuance.analogy: Temptation is like a magnet placed near a compass: it pulls hard even when you are trying to point somewhere else.
nuance.etymology: From Latin temptatio, from temptare 'to try, test, tempt'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the p in pronunciation; say 'temp-TAY-shun' with a clear p.
Saying 'I have a temptation' where 'I feel tempted' is more natural.
Using temptation for a simple choice; it implies a pull toward something you should avoid.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word peirasmos can mean testing, trial or temptation, depending on context. In Matthew 4:1 Jesus is led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, and James 1:13-14 says that God tempts no one and that each person is drawn away by his own desire. In 1 Corinthians 10:13 Paul says that no temptation has overtaken believers beyond what is common to humanity, and that God provides a way of escape. The Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6:13 asks God not to lead us into temptation.

senses.definition: A framework upon which cloth is stretched and dried.
One who takes care of, or tends, machines in a factory; a kind of assistant foreman.
senses.example: The old mill's tenter walked the floor each shift, checking that every loom was running smoothly.

senses.definition: A kind of governor, or regulating device.
senses.example: The steam engine's tenter adjusted the valve automatically to keep the speed constant.

senses.definition: To stretch cloth on such a framework.
senses.example: The workers tentered the wet linen across wooden frames so it would dry flat and straight.

senses.definition: To admit extension; to be stretchable.
senses.example: This knit fabric tenters well, so the cuffs stretch without losing their shape.

core.definition: A frame with hooks or clips on which wet cloth is stretched and dried so that it dries flat and even.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The t between two vowels is flapped in American speech, so the word sounds close to TEN-der; keep the n clear before it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized textile term, so it mainly appears in historical writing or the cloth trade and can sound unfamiliar to most Americans.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will meet this word only in the idiom 'on tenterhooks', meaning anxiously waiting, which is common and very useful. For the machine itself, modern textile plants usually say 'stenter' or 'tenter frame'. Do not use tenter for an everyday item.

distinctions.note: A tent is a portable shelter; a tenter is a frame for stretching cloth. The two words share a Latin root but not a meaning.
Stenter is the modern industrial term for a machine that stretches fabric; tenter is the older and more literary word.

examples.everyday: The docent showed us an old tenter, a wooden frame where the wool was stretched to dry.
examples.professional: The plant replaced the old tenter frames with a modern stenter line to speed up drying.
examples.analytical: By stretching cloth to a fixed width, the tenter shaped the economics of early English weaving.

nuance.analogy: Like a clothesline that pulls the fabric flat instead of letting it hang loose.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Medieval Latin, related to Latin tendere 'to stretch'; the exact path is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing tenter with tent, which is a different word with a different meaning.
Pronouncing the middle t as a hard t instead of the American flap.
Using tenter to mean a modern industrial machine without the proper term.

tenter.etymology: Via Old French, perhaps from Latin *tentorium*.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or restricted to a specific geographic area, or territory.
senses.example: The license is territorial, valid only within the county where the dentist practices.

senses.definition: Of or relating to geography or territory.
senses.example: The survey team compared the territorial boundaries on the old maps with satellite images.

senses.definition: Organized for home defense - such as the Territorial Army.
senses.example: During the war, my grandfather joined the territorial force guarding the coastline at night.

senses.definition: Displaying territoriality.
senses.example: Our cat becomes territorial whenever a new dog walks past the front window.

senses.definition: A non-professional member of a territorial army.
senses.example: My cousin, a territorial, trains one weekend a month and serves in the summer.

core.definition: Relating to a particular territory or area of land; also, protective of one's own space, property, or influence.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TOR, the third syllable, and the early syllables are weak. The final -al is a light uhl, not a full al sound, and the r in the middle must be clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in geographic, legal and biological use; negative or defensive when describing a person who guards their space or turf.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, territorial is used in geography, law and biology, as in territorial waters or territorial disputes, and for animals that defend an area. For people, it describes someone who guards their space or possessions, and it can sound critical. The British noun Territorial Army has no direct American equivalent; Americans would say the National Guard or the reserves.

distinctions.note: Territory is the noun for the land itself, while territorial is the adjective for something related to it.
Regional refers to a broad area of a country or the world, while territorial implies boundaries, control or defense.

examples.everyday: Our cat gets really territorial about the back porch.
examples.professional: Please avoid territorial behavior between the two teams and share the dashboards.
examples.analytical: The treaty settled the territorial claims that had divided the two empires for more than a century.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog marking a yard, a territorial person draws a line around what they consider theirs.
nuance.etymology: From Latin territorium, land around a town, from terra, land.
common_mistakes: Using territorial as a noun for a person, as in 'He is a territorial'; use the adjective with a noun
Stressing the first syllable, as in TER-ih-tor-ee-al, instead of the third

territorial.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin *territorialis*, from Latin *territorium*; equivalent to *territory* + *al*.

senses.definition: Statements made by a witness in court.
senses.example: The bookkeeper's testimony convinced the jury that the company had falsified its records.

senses.definition: An account of first-hand experience.
senses.example: Her testimony about surviving the flood moved everyone who heard her speak at the school.

senses.definition: In a church service (or religious service), a personal account, such as one's conversion, testimony of faith, or life testimony.
senses.example: During the Sunday service, Maria gave her testimony about how she came to faith.

senses.definition: Witness; evidence; proof of some fact.
senses.example: This new win is testimony to the tactical skill of their coach.

core.definition: A solemn statement of what a person witnessed or knows, given as evidence in court or as a personal account of faith.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TES. The second syllable is a reduced 'ih', and the final 'ny' is a light 'nee' sound. Learners often stress the -mo- syllable or add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal settings; serious and sometimes emotional in church settings, where it often means a personal account of faith.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use testimony most in courtrooms and legislative hearings, as in 'give testimony before Congress'. In churches it often means a short personal account of faith, sometimes called 'sharing a testimony'. In casual talk people say 'story' or 'account', though testimony carries more weight.

distinctions.note: A testimonial is a recommendation of someone's worth; testimony is a statement of what happened or what someone experienced.
Evidence is any material that supports a claim; testimony is evidence given by a person, spoken or written.

examples.everyday: My coworker shared her testimony at church last Sunday, and it moved a lot of people.
examples.professional: Her testimony before the subcommittee helped the team understand how the software bug reached customers.
examples.analytical: A testimony of faith is not mere autobiography; it claims that a personal life has been reshaped by a truth that exceeds it.

nuance.analogy: Testimony is like a witness stand for your life: you stand up and say honestly what you have seen and know.
nuance.etymology: From Latin testimonium, 'evidence', from testis, 'witness'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a testimony' in court; in court you give testimony, while 'a testimony' is mainly used for a religious personal account.
Stressing the -mo- syllable, as in tes-tih-MOH-nee.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the key word is 'edut, meaning testimony or witness, used for the covenant law and the ark of the covenant. In Greek the word is marturia, meaning witness or testimony. Exodus 31:18 describes God giving Moses the two tables of the testimony, the stone tablets of the law. John 5:31 has Jesus saying that if he bore witness only to himself, his testimony would not be true. Revelation 12:17 describes faithful believers who bear testimony to Jesus.

testimony.etymology: Middle English *testimonie*, from Old French *testimonie*, from Latin *testimōnium* (“testimony”).

senses.definition: Ellipsis of text message, a brief written message transmitted between mobile phones.
A writing consisting of multiple glyphs, characters, symbols or sentences.
senses.example: The printed text on the warning label was too small for my eyes to read.

senses.definition: A book, tome or other set of writings.
senses.example: The old library had a dusty text on medieval medicine that nobody had borrowed in decades.

senses.definition: Anything chosen as the subject of an argument, literary composition, etc.
senses.example: Our seminar's text for the week was a short essay on whether machines can reason.

senses.definition: Data which can be interpreted as human-readable text.
senses.example: Before training the model, I cleaned the text by removing HTML tags and emojis.

senses.definition: A verse or passage of Scripture, especially one chosen as the subject of a sermon, or in proof of a doctrine.
senses.example: The pastor based his sermon on a single text from the Gospel of John.

senses.definition: A style of writing in large characters; also, a kind of type used in printing.
senses.example: German text

senses.definition: To send a text message to; i.e. to transmit text using the Short Message Service (SMS), or a similar service, between communications devices, particularly mobile phones.
senses.example: Just text me when you get here.

senses.definition: To send and receive text messages.
senses.example: Have you been texting all afternoon?

senses.definition: (dated) To write in large characters, as in text hand.
senses.example: Back then, apprentices learned to text the headings of each page in large, careful letters.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A short written message sent electronically from one mobile phone to another.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable with a short e and a clean final cluster, /kst/. Do not add a vowel after the x sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and casual. In formal writing, people say 'message' or 'letter' instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use text as a noun for a text message ('I got a text from her') and as a verb ('text me when you land'). In professional settings, a quick text is fine for logistics, but anything substantive usually goes by email. The sense of written words in a book is separate and more formal.

distinctions.note: Message is general and can be spoken or written; text specifically means a typed message sent by phone.
Email goes through an email system and is usually longer and more formal than a text.

examples.everyday: Hey, can you send me a text when you get home?
examples.professional: I'll send you a text if the meeting moves to three o'clock.
examples.analytical: Studies of how teenagers coordinate plans by text show that very short messages can carry a surprising amount of social meaning.

nuance.analogy: A text is a postcard for your phone: short, quick and sent without the formality of a letter.
nuance.etymology: From Latin textus, 'woven thing', from texere, 'to weave'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'text to him' instead of 'text him' or 'send him a text'.
Confusing text (a message) with textbook or texture.

conversation.text: Text me when you get home.
I got a text from the bank saying my card was used.
The text on this slide is too small to read.

senses.definition: A subdivision of currency, equal to one hundredth of a pula.

core.definition: A small unit of money in Botswana, equal to one hundredth of a pula.

pronunciation.tip: The initial th is a plain t sound, aspirated (a small puff of air), not the English 'th' of 'the.' Stress falls on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term for a currency unit, with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely encounter thebe unless they travel to Botswana, deal with its currency, or study African economies. In conversation you would usually mention the pula and say the change came in thebe, in the way a traveler might say cents. There is no American equivalent word, so the term is simply used as is.

distinctions.note: The pula is the main unit of Botswana's currency, while the thebe is its smaller subunit, worth one hundredth of a pula.
The cent is the subunit of the US dollar; the thebe plays a similar role for the pula, but it is a different currency.

examples.everyday: The cashier gave me a few thebe in change, so I'm keeping them as a souvenir.
examples.professional: Our finance team converts supplier invoices from Gaborone and reports the amounts in pula and thebe.
examples.analytical: Botswana's decimal currency divides the pula into one hundred thebe, a structure that parallels the dollar and the cent.

nuance.analogy: A thebe is to the pula what a cent is to the dollar: a small piece that makes up the whole.
nuance.etymology: From Setswana, the language of Botswana, where thebe means 'shield.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial th as the English voiced 'th' in 'the' instead of a t sound.
Treating thebe as an English word for a coin and assuming the same spelling for a plural form.
Confusing thebe with the pula, which is the main unit of currency.

senses.definition: To think about a time or experience; to recall.
senses.example: When I think back on those times we shared together, I can't help but feel a little sad.

core.definition: To remember a past time, event, or person by mentally returning to it.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BACK. Use the short a sound in back, as in 'cat', not the 'ah' sound of 'father'. The final k is clear in think.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to warm. It often introduces nostalgic or reflective memories.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use think back to when or think back on to introduce a memory, often a fond or reflective one. It is common in storytelling, in meetings about past projects, and in conversations with old friends. Saying 'remember when' is a casual alternative.

distinctions.note: Remember is the general word, while think back emphasizes actively returning mentally to a past period.
Reminisce means talking or thinking about pleasant past times, so it is more about enjoyment, while think back can be neutral.
Recall is more formal and often used for retrieving specific facts or details.

examples.everyday: When I think back to our first apartment, it was tiny, but we loved it.
examples.professional: Thinking back to our first sprint, we underestimated how long the testing would take.
examples.analytical: If we think back over the history of this doctrine, we can see how its emphasis shifted across centuries.

nuance.analogy: Like rewinding a tape to find the exact spot where the song began.
nuance.etymology: Think from Old English thencan, and back from Old English bæc.
common_mistakes: Dropping the preposition, as in 'I think back the summer' instead of 'I think back to the summer'.
Pronouncing back with the vowel of 'father' rather than the short a of 'cat'.

senses.definition: A person who is a member of a gang or criminal organization.
senses.example: Police arrested three thugs from the gang after the warehouse robbery.

senses.definition: A violent, aggressive, or truculent person.
A criminal that extorts people.
senses.example: The shop owner paid weekly to thugs who threatened to burn his store.

senses.definition: A person who use intimidation to coerce others.
One who, usually as a result of social disadvantage, has turned to committing crimes (e.g. selling drugs, robbery, assault, etc.) to make a living; a gangsta.
senses.example: Critics argue that poverty, not character, turns many young men into thugs.

senses.definition: An overvigorous plant that spreads and dominates the flowerbed.
senses.example: The mint in the garden bed became a thug, choking every other herb.

senses.definition: A wooden bat used in the game of miniten, fitting around the player's hand.
senses.example: Players in miniten swung the wooden thug, which fitted snugly around the hand.

senses.definition: (historical) One of a band of assassins formerly active in northern India who worshipped Kali and sacrificed their victims to her.
senses.example: Colonial records describe how thugs strangled travelers on roads in northern India.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To commit acts of thuggery, to live the life of a thug, to menace, to commit crime.
senses.example: The gang began to thug the shopkeepers, demanding cash and threatening their families.

senses.definition: To appear as a thug; to dress and act in a manner reminiscent of a thug.
senses.example: He started to thug around the block in a hooded jacket, trying to look tough.

core.definition: A violent or rough criminal, or a person who uses intimidation and force to get what they want.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'u' as in 'bug' and a hard 'g' at the end. Don't add a vowel after the 'g,' and keep the 'th' voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative: it describes someone as violent or intimidating, and it can carry racial or class bias when used loosely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thug' in news, politics, sports, and casual talk for people who commit violence or intimidate others. It is a strong insult, so using it for a rival or a political opponent can sound harsh. The verb form exists but is rare in everyday American speech. A thoughtful speaker chooses words carefully when using it, since it can stereotype people.

distinctions.note: A bully intimidates weaker people, often without serious violence, while a thug is more openly violent or criminal.
A hooligan is a rowdy troublemaker, often a sports fan who causes disorder, while a thug is more dangerous and criminal.
A gangster belongs to organized crime, while 'thug' is a broader and more insulting term for violent people.

examples.everyday: Two thugs tried to rob the man outside the gas station, but the police arrived in time.
examples.professional: The manager's thuggish tone in the meeting made people afraid to speak up.
examples.analytical: Critics describe the regime's enforcers as thugs, a label that hides the institutional structure behind their violence.

nuance.analogy: Like a wolf in a pack: the danger is in the group's willingness to use force against others.
nuance.etymology: From Hindi ṭhag, meaning swindler or robber, referring to a gang of robbers and murderers in India.
common_mistakes: Adding a vowel, as in 'thuh-guh,' instead of a single short syllable.
Using 'thug' as a neutral word for a tough athlete, which can sound offensive.
Confusing the noun with the verb, which is rare in everyday speech.

senses.definition: Again and again; repeatedly; every time; always; time and again.
senses.example: Time after time he tries, and time and again, he fails.

core.definition: Again and again, repeatedly, on many separate occasions.

pronunciation.tip: The last word, time, carries the main stress. The middle word after is weak, so the second vowel reduces to a light 'ur' and the t is flapped, sounding almost like a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can praise someone's reliability ('she helped us time after time') or express frustration ('he makes the same mistake time after time').
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in everyday speech and informal writing to describe something that keeps happening. It often appears with complaints, so it can sound annoyed. There is no set reply; people simply respond to the point being made.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly interchangeable, but time after time often feels more conversational and emphasizes each separate occasion.
Over and over often stresses repeating the same action, while time after time emphasizes the recurrence of an outcome or event over a longer period.

collocations: I've told you time after time
the team won time after time
the same question time after time

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog keeps digging up my tulips, time after time.
examples.professional: The deployment pipeline failed time after time, so we added automatic retries and better alerts.
examples.analytical: Time after time, the historical record shows that reform movements begin with moral urgency and end in institutional compromise.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock that strikes the same hour again and again, the event keeps returning on schedule.
common_mistakes: Saying 'time by time' instead of 'time after time.'
Using it for a single event; it requires repeated occurrences.

senses.definition: Lacking in courage or confidence.
senses.example: John's a very timid person. I doubt he'll be brave enough to face his brother.

core.definition: Easily frightened or shy, lacking courage or self-confidence in ordinary situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the i in both syllables is short, as in 'bit.' The word does not rhyme with 'tie-mid,' which is a common learner error.

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly negative; it describes a personality trait, though a gentle timid person may be described kindly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use timid for people who hesitate to speak up, try new things, or take risks. Saying someone is timid is a fairly direct judgment, so use it carefully about colleagues. For a shy person, people often say shy or reserved.

distinctions.note: Shy describes discomfort around other people, while timid describes a general lack of courage to act or speak.
Cautious suggests careful, reasoned prudence, while timid suggests fear that holds someone back.

examples.everyday: She gave a timid knock on the door, not sure anyone was home.
examples.professional: Our junior engineers were too timid to challenge the roadmap in meetings, so the risks went unspoken.
examples.analytical: The author describes the timid reader as one who avoids hard texts, which turns intellectual caution into a moral failing.

nuance.analogy: Timid is like a turtle that pulls its head in at the first noise: it is not stupid, just too afraid to move forward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin timidus, from timere, to fear.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long i, as in 'TIE-mid'.
Using timid when shy is more accurate for someone who is socially uncomfortable but confident in their work.

timid.etymology: From Middle French *timide*, from Latin *timidus* (“full of fear, fearful, timid”), from *timeō* (“to fear”).

senses.definition: Of, relating to, being, derived from, or having a title.
senses.example: The titular head of the company has no real power over daily operations.

senses.definition: Existing in name only; nominal.
Named or referred to in the title.
senses.example: Macbeth is a titular character.

senses.definition: One who holds a title.
senses.example: The titular of the duchy still attends ceremonies but has no political authority.

senses.definition: The person from whom a church takes its special name; distinguished from a patron, who must be canonized or an angel.
senses.example: Our parish is a titular church, named for Saint Mary, and its feast is celebrated every August.

core.definition: Existing in name only; holding a title or position without real power or duties.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle sound is 'ch', as in 'church', and the last syllable is a reduced, rhotic 'er'. Do not say 'TIT-yoo-lar'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when describing a leader who lacks real authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use titular in news, politics, and business to describe someone who has a title but little real power, such as a titular head of state. In casual speech people more often say figurehead or in name only. Using it in a conversation with friends can sound formal, but it is natural in analysis and journalism.

distinctions.note: Nominal stresses that something exists in name or on paper, while titular stresses that someone holds a title with no real authority.
Honorary describes a title given as a tribute, often without duties, while titular describes a title that exists without real power in practice.

examples.everyday: My uncle is the titular president of the club, but his daughter actually runs everything.
examples.professional: The board named her the titular chair, while the operating decisions went to the CEO.
examples.analytical: The constitution made the monarch the titular head of state, leaving the real power of government with elected officials.

nuance.analogy: A titular leader is like a flag on a building: it marks the place and carries a name, but it does not run the building.
nuance.etymology: From Latin titulus, 'title, inscription'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'TIT-yoo-lar' with a 'yoo' sound, which is not standard American.
Confusing titular with entitled, which means having a right to something.

titular.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *titulaire*, from Latin *titulāris*, from *titulus* (“title”).

senses.definition: A system that parses an input stream into its component tokens.

core.definition: A program or component that splits an input stream, such as text, into the tokens a computer will process.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllables light. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so say 'zer' with the r clearly heard, not 'zuh' or 'zah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tokenizer for a specific tool, such as the component that comes with a language model or a library. People often say 'the tokenizer' to mean the tool attached to a model. Compiler engineers may say lexer instead.

distinctions.note: A lexer is a lexical analyzer from compiler design, while tokenizer is the more general term used in machine learning and text processing.
A tokenizer breaks input into units, while a parser builds a structure from those units.

examples.everyday: The app uses the same tokenizer as the model, so the word counts match.
examples.professional: We need to update the tokenizer before deploying the new model, or the vocabulary won't match.
examples.analytical: A tokenizer embeds assumptions about what counts as a word, and those assumptions shape the model's behavior across languages.

nuance.analogy: Like a sorting machine at a post office that places each letter into its own bin.
nuance.etymology: From tokenize plus the agent suffix -er; token is from Old English tācen, sign.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'toh-kuh-NY-zer'.
Dropping the final r, so it sounds like 'tokenize-uh'.

conversation.text: The tokenizer converts raw text into integer IDs from a fixed vocabulary before the model sees anything.
Some of the arithmetic errors came from the tokenizer splitting long numbers into odd chunks.
Many tokenizers are less efficient on languages like Amharic, so the same sentence takes far more tokens than in English.

senses.definition: Appearing to be exceptionally good, and therefore arousing suspicion of illegitimacy.
senses.example: He wants to give you two million dollars? That's just too good to be true!

core.definition: Seeming so favorable that it is probably false, unrealistic, or a scam.

pronunciation.tip: Reduce 'to' to 'tuh' or 'tu' in speech, and make 'be' short as 'bee'. The r in 'true' is strong in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautious. It signals suspicion, and it can suggest that someone should check the facts before trusting an offer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a deal, offer, or story sounds too favorable to trust, often in shopping, investing, or online messages. It is a warning, not praise. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I thought the same thing' or 'Let's check it out first'.

distinctions.note: Sounds fishy is more informal and suggests something is suspicious, while too good to be true focuses on the offer being unrealistically favorable.
Unbelievable can be a compliment or an exclamation, while too good to be true is a warning about deception.

collocations: sounds too good to be true
a deal too good to be true
that's too good to be true
seemed too good to be true
an offer too good to be true

examples.everyday: A guy on the street offered me a new phone for fifty bucks, but it sounded too good to be true.
examples.professional: The vendor promised a forty percent cost cut with no downtime, which is too good to be true, so let's pilot it first.
examples.analytical: A proposal that promises certainty without cost is often too good to be true, and philosophers have long been wary of such claims.

nuance.analogy: It is like a sign in a shop window that says everything is free: you check the fine print before you believe it.
common_mistakes: Using it as praise for something very impressive, when it actually signals suspicion.
Saying 'too good to be true' without the final 'true' sound, which is part of the idiom.

conversation.text: A free cruise? That sounds too good to be true.
The job offer seemed too good to be true, and it was a scam.
If the results look too good to be true, check the data again.

senses.definition: The noise of a horn or whistle.
senses.example: He gave a little toot of the horn, to get their attention.

senses.definition: A fart; flatus.
senses.example: Sorry, everyone, that little toot at dinner was mine, not the dog's.

senses.definition: Cocaine.
senses.example: Police said the dealer had hidden a bag of toot in the car.

senses.definition: A portion of cocaine that a person snorts.
senses.example: He took one last toot in the bathroom before the party started.

senses.definition: A spree of drunkenness.
senses.example: After the layoff, he went on a toot that lasted three days.

senses.definition: Rubbish; tat.
senses.example: I'm not paying fifty pounds for this load of old toot!

senses.definition: A message on the social networking software Mastodon.
senses.example: I posted a toot about the new library release, and it got boosted fast.

senses.definition: A small child; alternative form of tot.
senses.example: Look at that little toot, already walking across the kitchen floor!

senses.definition: To stand out, or be prominent.
senses.example: Her red scarf toots against the gray snow in the park.

senses.definition: To peep; to look narrowly.
senses.example: She tooted through the blinds to see who was knocking at the door.

senses.definition: To see; to spy.
senses.example: Hiding behind the hedge, he tooted the deer grazing near the creek.

senses.definition: To produce the noise of a horn or whistle.
senses.example: The old ferry tooted twice as it pulled away from the dock.

senses.definition: To cause a horn or whistle to produce a noise.
senses.example: Dad tooted the car horn twice to tell the kids we were leaving.

senses.definition: To flatulate.
senses.example: The dog tooted loudly under the table during the whole dinner.

senses.definition: Of a queen bee, to make a high-pitched sound during certain stages of development.
senses.example: Before the workers emerge, the queen tooted from inside her cell.

senses.definition: To go on a drinking binge.
senses.example: After the game, the guys tooted all night and nobody drove home.

senses.definition: To snort (a recreational drug).
senses.example: He tooted a line in the restroom and came back twitching.

senses.definition: To post a message on a Mastodon instance.
senses.example: She tooted a photo of the sunrise from the summit this morning.

core.definition: A short, sharp blast of sound from a horn, whistle, or similar instrument.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long, tense oo sound with a clear t at the end. Do not confuse it with 'tout', which has a different vowel and means to promote something.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful when describing sound, but negative or crude when used for a flatulence sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'toot' for a short horn or whistle, often for children, trains, or a friendly car horn. Slang for flatulence is informal and can be rude in mixed company. The idiom 'toot your own horn' means to brag, and it can sound critical. A natural reply to a train whistle is simply to smile or wave.

distinctions.note: 'Honk' is typically a car horn sound, while 'toot' is a shorter or softer whistle or horn sound, often from a train or a child's toy.
'Tout' means to promote something loudly, and it sounds different, with a diphthong; 'toot' is a short blast.

examples.everyday: The train gave a long toot as it pulled into the station, and the kids waved.
examples.professional: Please give a short toot on the horn before you enter the blind corner, so the crew knows you're there.
examples.analytical: The review shifts from measured analysis into a toot of self-congratulation, which weakens its credibility.

nuance.analogy: A toot is like a small bugle call: short, bright, and meant to get attention.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of a short horn or whistle sound, first recorded in the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'toot' with 'tout'; 'toot' means a horn sound, while 'tout' means to promote.
Using the slang meaning of flatulence in polite company without awareness that it is rude.

senses.definition: Having or consisting of a top; covered with a top layer.
senses.example: The sandwiches were topped with pickles and sliced tomatoes.

core.definition: Covered on the upper surface with something, such as a layer of food or decoration, often used with 'with'.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable ending in a clear 't' sound. Don't add a vowel and say 'tap-ed,' and don't drop the final t sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when used about food, and it suggests something extra or appealing has been added on top.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'topped with' constantly for food, as in 'a burger topped with bacon' or 'ice cream topped with hot fudge.' It is an everyday menu word. In a restaurant you will often see it in descriptions, and a natural spoken reply is 'Sounds good!'

distinctions.note: Covered means hidden completely under something, while topped means a layer sits on the upper surface, often as decoration.
Topped off is a phrasal verb that means finished or filled to the top, so it is not the same as describing a finished food with a topping.

examples.everyday: I'll have the pancakes, topped with bananas and maple syrup, please.
examples.professional: The dashboard is topped with a summary panel that shows the three key metrics for the quarter.
examples.analytical: Each stanza is topped by a refrain that shifts the meaning of the whole poem as the reader returns to it.

nuance.analogy: Like a cupcake with a swirl of frosting on the top, where the frosting sits on the surface and doesn't change the cake inside.
nuance.etymology: From top (verb) plus the past participle suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Saying 'topped of' instead of 'topped with' when naming the topping.
Adding an extra vowel at the end, pronouncing it as 'tap-ed.'

senses.definition: A neume denoting a set of three tones which first rise from the original tone, then fall.

core.definition: In medieval and Gregorian chant notation, a single sign of three notes that rises from the first note and then falls.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOR, and the r is pronounced after the vowel, so don't say 'tawk.' The unstressed final syllables are reduced to a quick 'uh' and 'us.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. It is used only in musicology and chant study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only among musicologists, chant scholars, church musicians and students of medieval manuscripts. In everyday talk you would just say 'a neume' or 'a note group.' The term is precise and not used casually.

distinctions.note: A porrectus is a sign that falls and then rises, the reverse of the torculus's rise and fall.
A climacus is a sign of descending notes, while a torculus goes up and then down.

collocations: rise and fall of the torculus

examples.everyday: I can't read chant notation, but the choir director pointed at a torculus on the page and said to sing it as one smooth arc.
examples.professional: In this manuscript each torculus is written as one ligature, so the singers should phrase the three notes as a single group.
examples.analytical: The torculus, with its rise and fall around a central pivot, shows how medieval scribes encoded melodic direction within a single sign.

nuance.analogy: Like a small arch, which climbs up to a peak and then comes back down, in one continuous shape.
nuance.etymology: From Latin torculus, 'small press,' a diminutive of torcular, 'winepress.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in tor-KYOO-lus.
Confusing torculus with porrectus, which has the opposite shape.

senses.definition: In AI: In reinforcement learning, the sequence of states, actions and rewards in one episode.
The path an object takes as it moves.
The ordered set of intermediate states assumed by a dynamical system as a result of time evolution.
senses.example: The model computes the trajectory of the system through phase space at each timestep.

senses.definition: A course of development, such as that of a war or career.
The path of a body as it travels through space.

core.definition: The path an object follows through the air or space, or the course of development over time (a career trajectory); in reinforcement learning, the sequence of states, actions and rewards an agent experiences in one episode.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, JEK. The first syllable is weak, so say 'truh' rather than 'tra', and the final -ory is a quick 'uh-ree'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a path or pattern without judging whether it is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI, trajectory usually means the recorded path of an episode or a sequence of states. In everyday American speech it means the general direction of something over time, such as a career or a company's trajectory. A common phrase in meetings is 'if we stay on this trajectory,' meaning 'if things continue this way.'

distinctions.note: Path is general and neutral; trajectory emphasizes a course that follows a measurable or predictable pattern over time.
Course is everyday for a direction or plan; trajectory suggests a pattern you can plot and extend into the future.
In reinforcement learning an episode is one complete run, while a trajectory is the recorded sequence of states, actions, and rewards within that episode.

examples.everyday: Our sales are on a good trajectory this year, so I'm not worried.
examples.professional: The debugging script logs every agent trajectory so we can see where the policy starts to go wrong.
examples.analytical: Each trajectory in the training batch is a sample from the policy's distribution over state-action sequences, which determines the variance of the gradient estimate.

nuance.analogy: A trajectory is like a GPS breadcrumb trail: each point records where you were and what you did, so the whole route is visible.
nuance.etymology: From Neo-Latin trajectoria, from Latin trajicere, 'to throw across', from trans-, across, and jacere, 'to throw'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable or saying 'TRAJ-ik-tor-ee' with a hard j and long a; the stress is on JEK.
Using trajectory for a single static position; it implies movement over time.

trajectory.etymology: From New Latin *trāiectōria* (“trajectory”), the feminine of *trāiectōrius* (“of or pertaining to throwing across”), from Latin *trāiectus* (“thrown over or across”), past participle of *trāiciō*, from *trans-* (“across, beyond”) (see *trans-*) + *iaciō*…

conversation.text: A trajectory is the sequence of states, actions, and rewards from one run of the policy.
We reviewed failed agent trajectories to see where the plan went wrong.
Her career trajectory changed when she moved from analytics into machine learning.

senses.definition: To exceed or overstep some limit or boundary.
senses.example: The runner transgressed the boundary line and was disqualified from the race.

senses.definition: To act in violation of some law.
senses.example: Anyone who transgresses the new zoning law may face fines and a court summons.

senses.definition: To commit an offense; to sin.
senses.example: Many believers ask how God forgives those who transgress against their own consciences.

senses.definition: To spread over land along a shoreline; to inundate.
senses.example: Each spring the rising tide transgresses the low dunes and spreads across the marsh.

core.definition: To break a rule, law, or moral principle, or to go beyond a limit that someone has set or that is considered acceptable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, GRES. The 'ns' cluster is pronounced as 'nz' here, so say 'tranz', not 'trans', before the 'g'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies breaking a rule, law or boundary, often with a sense of moral wrongdoing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'transgress' in formal writing, news reports about laws, religious discussions, or literature. In everyday speech, they would say 'break the rules' or 'cross the line'. The word is often used with 'against' or 'the boundaries of,' as in 'transgress against the community.'

distinctions.note: Violate is the everyday word for breaking a rule or law; transgress is more formal and often implies crossing a moral or social boundary.
Break is general and casual; transgress is elevated and suggests a deliberate step beyond an accepted limit.

examples.everyday: Parking in the fire lane is a clear way to transgress the rules of the building.
examples.professional: If an employee transgresses the company's data policy, HR will review the case within a week.
examples.analytical: In the Gospels, Jesus is accused of transgressing the traditions of the elders, and his response reframes what the law actually requires.

nuance.analogy: To transgress is like stepping over a painted line on a field; you go past the boundary that everyone agreed to respect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transgredi, from trans- 'across' and gradi 'to step'; the root meaning is 'to step across'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'trans' instead of 'tranz'.
Using 'transgress' with 'to' as in 'transgress to'; the usual pattern is 'transgress against' or 'transgress the boundary'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew Scripture, the idea of transgression is often expressed by pesha', meaning rebellion or revolt against God, and in the New Testament by parabainō, meaning to step across a line or to violate a command. Matthew 15:2 uses parabainō when the scribes and Pharisees accuse the disciples of transgressing the tradition of the elders. Galatians 2:18 uses the related noun to describe a person who builds again what he has torn down and so proves himself a transgressor.

transgress.etymology: From Middle English *transgressen*, from Old French *transgresser* and Latin *transgressus*, past participle of *transgredior*.

senses.definition: Able to be transmitted.
Capable of being transmitted from a transmitter to a receiver.
senses.example: Engineers tested whether the encrypted signal remained transmissible through the damaged cable.

senses.definition: Able to transmit a disease; infectious, contagious.
senses.example: Health officials warned that the new strain is highly transmissible among young children.

senses.definition: Capable of being transmitted from one person to another.
senses.example: Researchers study whether this particular belief is transmissible from parents to their children.

core.definition: Able to be passed from one person, place or thing to another, especially a disease that can spread from person to person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MIS. The ss is a plain /s/, not a /z/, and the ending -ible is a reduced vowel plus l, so it sounds like uh-buhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use, but usually negative when describing a disease or harmful agent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transmissible mainly in medical, scientific and public health writing, as in highly transmissible virus or transmissible infection. In everyday conversation they say contagious, which sounds more natural. For messages, files or data, Americans prefer transmittable.

distinctions.note: Contagious is the everyday word for a disease spread by contact; transmissible is more technical and describes the capacity of an agent to be passed on.
Transmittable is the usual choice for messages, data or files, while transmissible is preferred for diseases and genetic traits.

examples.everyday: The doctor says this stomach bug is really transmissible, so wash your hands a lot and stay home until you feel better.
examples.professional: The new variant is more transmissible, so our public health team is updating the masking guidance for the clinics.
examples.analytical: A pathogen is transmissible only if its particles can move from one host to another under ordinary conditions of contact.

nuance.analogy: A transmissible disease is like a cold passed along a crowded bus: it moves from person to person by a simple route.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transmissibilis, from transmittere, to send across.
common_mistakes: Using transmissible for messages or data, where transmittable is the usual American word.
Pronouncing the ss as /z/ instead of /s/.

senses.definition: A worker who collects and hauls away household or municipal garbage, often using a truck to transport it for processing or disposal.
senses.example: The trashman wheeled our bins to the curb every Tuesday morning before sunrise.

core.definition: A person who collects household garbage from curbside bins and hauls it away on a truck.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable carries the main stress. The vowel in man is the short a of 'cat', not the 'uh' of 'mun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly informal; many workers prefer the term sanitation worker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say trashman in casual talk, especially for the crew that comes to the house on a set day. Many people now say garbage collector or sanitation worker, and official documents use those terms. Sanitation worker is the most respectful choice, so treat the worker with the same courtesy you would give a neighbor.

distinctions.note: Garbage collector is a common neutral term, while trashman is more casual.
Sanitation worker is the official and respectful term used by cities and employers, more formal than trashman.

examples.everyday: The trashman always waves when he drives past our house on Thursday mornings.
examples.professional: We are working with the city's sanitation department to adjust the pickup schedule over the holiday week.
examples.analytical: The work of collecting trash is invisible until it stops, which is why cities treat collection as essential infrastructure.

nuance.analogy: The trashman is like a quiet janitor for the whole neighborhood, showing up on schedule and removing what everyone else discards.
nuance.etymology: A compound of trash and man, a common informal American formation.
common_mistakes: Using trashman in formal writing where sanitation worker is expected
Stressing man instead of trash in the compound

senses.definition: A polygon with three sides and three angles.
senses.example: The student proved that the interior angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.

senses.definition: A set square.
senses.example: He used a plastic triangle to draw a perfect 45-degree line on the drafting paper.

senses.definition: A love triangle.
senses.example: The novel's love triangle between the two sisters and their neighbor kept me reading.

senses.definition: The structure of systems composed with three interrelated objects.
senses.example: Our recommendation model is a triangle of users, products, and reviews that updates together.

senses.definition: A draughtsman's square in the form of a right-angled triangle.
senses.example: Use the triangle's right angle to check that the wall is square before you nail it.

senses.definition: Any of various large papilionid butterflies of the genus Graphium.
senses.example: The museum's collection included a striking triangle butterfly from the rainforests of Southeast Asia.

senses.definition: A triangular formation of railway tracks, with a curve on at least one side.
senses.example: The freight trains turned around at the rail triangle before heading back to the yard.

senses.definition: A percussion instrument made by forming a metal rod into a triangular shape which is open at one angle. It is suspended from a string and hit with a metal bar to make a resonant sound.
senses.example: The orchestra's triangle player waited twelve bars before striking one bright clear note.

senses.definition: A triangular piece of equipment used for gathering the balls into the formation required by the game being played.
senses.example: The bartender racked the balls with a plastic triangle before the final game of the night.

senses.definition: (historical) A frame formed of three poles stuck in the ground and united at the top, to which people were bound for corporal punishment.
senses.example: In colonial times, offenders were sometimes tied to a triangle and whipped in the town square.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To form or be included in a three-part interaction, e.g. a Karpman drama triangle, such as by being ganged up on by two people or being torn between conflicting demands from two sources.
senses.example: Whenever the couple argued, their son somehow got triangled into every fight.

core.definition: A flat closed shape with three straight sides and three angles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable TRY-, and the second syllable 'ang' is short, not 'ahn'. The final 'gl' is one quick unstressed syllable 'guhl', not 'gell'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a basic word for a shape and is also used figuratively for three-part relationships.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use triangle for the basic shape in school and everyday life, and for triangular objects such as a slice of cheese or a metal percussion instrument. Figuratively it appears in phrases like 'love triangle' or 'trade triangle'. In geometry, the key features are three sides and three angles, and a right triangle has one 90-degree angle.

distinctions.note: Triangle is the noun for the figure; triangular is the adjective describing something with that shape.
Trilateral means having three sides or involving three parties, and is more formal or technical than triangle.
An angle is formed where two lines or sides meet, while a triangle is a closed figure made of three sides and three angles.

examples.everyday: The kids drew a big red triangle on top of a square house.
examples.professional: Can we add a triangle to the slide showing how the three teams depend on each other?
examples.analytical: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

nuance.analogy: A triangle is the simplest stable shape: three sides lock together so the frame resists collapsing, which is why bicycle frames use them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'triangulum', from 'tri-' (three) and 'angulus' (angle).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'tri-ANG-gle'.
Using the noun as an adjective, as in 'a triangle sandwich'; say 'a triangular sandwich'.

triangle.etymology: From Middle English *triangle*, from Old French *triangle*, from Latin *triangulum*, noun use of adjective *triangulus* (“three-cornered, having three angles”), from *trēs* (“three”) + *angulus* (“corner, angle”), equivalent to.

senses.definition: Involving three foci.
Of or pertaining to corrective lenses that have three different powers per eye.

core.definition: Having three different focal powers, usually in one lens, so you can see things far, near, and at middle distance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TRY, and reduce the last syllable to a light schwa, so it sounds like 'TRY-foh-kuhl,' not 'tri-FOH-cul.' The first r is rhotic and the o is a long 'oh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a product or optical feature without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trifocal mostly for eyeglasses, saying 'I need trifocals' or 'trifocal lenses.' Many people now prefer progressive lenses, which blend the zones without visible lines. In everyday talk, 'bifocals' is more common, and 'trifocals' is the specific term for three zones.

distinctions.note: Bifocals have two zones, usually for distance and reading; trifocals add a middle zone for computer or arm's-length vision.
Progressive lenses change power smoothly with no visible lines, while trifocals have distinct segments with visible boundaries.

examples.everyday: My grandfather finally switched to trifocals because he could never see his phone and the TV at the same time.
examples.professional: The optometrist recommended trifocal lenses for the patient, since the office work involves screens, documents, and driving.
examples.analytical: A trifocal lens divides the optical surface into three discrete zones, each with a fixed power, which forces the wearer to use the correct region for each distance.

nuance.analogy: Like a three-speed bike, each zone is a gear for one distance, and you shift by moving your eyes to the right part of the lens.
nuance.etymology: From tri- 'three' and focal, from Latin focus 'hearth, focal point'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'trifocal' for progressive lenses, which have no visible lines.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'tri-FOH-cal'.

senses.definition: The luggage storage compartment of a sedan/saloon-style car.
senses.example: We loaded the groceries into the trunk of the sedan and drove home.

senses.definition: A storage compartment fitted behind the seat of a motorcycle.
senses.example: He strapped his helmet into the trunk behind the seat of his motorcycle.

senses.definition: The usually single, more or less upright part of a tree, between the roots and the branches.
senses.example: The oak's trunk was so wide that three people could not reach around it.

senses.definition: In software projects under source control: the most current source tree, from which the latest unstable builds (so-called "trunk builds") are compiled.
senses.example: Please merge the fix into trunk before the nightly build runs tomorrow morning.

senses.definition: Part of a body.
senses.example: The physical therapist asked him to rotate his trunk slowly from side to side.

senses.definition: The torso; especially, the human torso.
senses.example: The shirt was tight across his broad chest and muscular trunk.

senses.definition: The conspicuously extended, mobile, nose-like organ of an animal such as a sengi, a tapir or especially an elephant. The trunks of various kinds of animals might be adapted to probing and sniffing, as in the sengis, or be partly prehensile, as in the tapir, or be a versatile prehensile organ for manipulation, feeding, drinking and fighting as in the elephant.
senses.example: The elephant curled its trunk around the bundle of hay and lifted it to its mouth.

senses.definition: A container.
senses.example: The museum displayed a carved wooden trunk filled with silver coins.

senses.definition: A large suitcase, chest, or similar receptacle for carrying or storing personal possessions, usually with a hinged, often domed lid, and handles at each end, so that generally it takes two persons to carry a full trunk.
senses.example: Grandmother's trunk sat at the foot of the bed, packed with quilts and letters.

senses.definition: A box or chest usually covered with leather, metal, or cloth, or sometimes made of leather, hide, or metal, for holding or transporting clothes or other goods.
senses.example: The leather trunk held our winter clothes in the attic all year long.

senses.definition: A channel for flow of some kind.
senses.example: The engineers widened the trunk to carry more water from the reservoir.

senses.definition: A major circuit between telephone switchboards or other switching equipment.
senses.example: The phone company upgraded the trunk lines connecting the two central offices.

senses.definition: A chute or conduit, or a watertight shaft connecting two or more decks.
senses.example: The crew climbed down the trunk to reach the lower deck during the storm.

senses.definition: A long, large box, pipe, or conductor, made of plank or metal plates, for various uses, as for conveying air to a mine or to a furnace, water to a mill, grain to an elevator, etc.
senses.example: The workers laid a wooden trunk to carry fresh air deep into the mine shaft.

senses.definition: A flume or sluice in which ores are separated from the slimes in which they are contained.
senses.example: The miners washed the crushed gravel through a trunk to separate the gold.

senses.definition: The main line or body of anything.
senses.example: the trunk of a vein or of an artery, as distinct from the branches

senses.definition: A main line in a river, canal, railroad, or highway system.
senses.example: The railroad's main trunk runs straight from Chicago to Denver across the plains.

senses.definition: A large pipe forming the piston rod of a steam engine, of sufficient diameter to allow one end of the connecting rod to be attached to the crank, and the other end to pass within the pipe directly to the piston, thus making the engine more compact.
Ellipsis of swimming trunks.
The part of a pilaster between the base and capital, corresponding to the shaft of a column.
To extract (ores) from the slimes in which they are contained, by means of a trunk.
To provide simultaneous network access to multiple clients by sharing a set of circuits, carriers, channels, or frequencies.

core.definition: The enclosed storage area at the back of a car, or the main thick stem of a tree.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a clear ng followed by k. Do not insert a vowel between ng and k, and do not pronounce the final k as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, practical word for a car part or a tree part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say trunk for the rear storage compartment of a car, which British speakers call the boot. In casual speech, people say open the trunk or put it in the trunk. For a tree, trunk is the everyday word for the main stem; Americans also use it for an elephant's nose, but that is a specialized sense.

distinctions.note: Boot is the British term for a car's rear storage area, while Americans say trunk.
A stump is the short base left after a tree is cut down, while a trunk is the living upright stem.

examples.everyday: Can you pop the trunk so I can put these grocery bags in?
examples.professional: The trunk of our rental car had no room for the sample cases, so we rented a van.
examples.analytical: The trunk of the tree, drawing water and nutrients between root and crown, is the axis around which the whole organism is structured.

nuance.analogy: A car trunk is like a closet built into the back of a car: a closed space for things you want out of sight while you drive.
nuance.etymology: From Old French tronc, from Latin truncus, trunk or stem.
common_mistakes: Saying the boot of the car, which sounds British to Americans.
Confusing trunk with trunks, which means swimming trunks or shorts.

trunk.etymology: From Middle English *tronke*, *trunke*, from Old French *tronc* (“alms box, tree trunk, headless body”), from Latin *truncus* (“a stock, lopped tree trunk”), from *truncus* (“cut off, maimed, mutilated”).

conversation.text: Throw your suitcase in the trunk, and let's go.
Can you pop the trunk? I need to grab my jacket.
A huge tree trunk fell across the road during the storm.

senses.definition: Wearing a turban.

core.definition: Wearing a turban, a long cloth wound around the head.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, pronounce the first vowel as an r-colored sound, and end with a clear d sound, not a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when used descriptively. It can sound stereotyping or exotic if used to single out someone by religion or ethnicity without need.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use turbaned in writing, news, and descriptions of art or history. In conversation, people usually say wearing a turban or simply describe the person's clothing. Use it with care, because Sikh and Muslim men who wear turbans may find it reductive if it becomes their only label.

distinctions.note: Hatted is a general term for wearing any hat, while turbaned names a specific head covering wound from cloth.
Bareheaded means having no covering on the head at all, so it is the direct opposite of turbaned.

examples.everyday: We saw a turbaned street musician playing near the fountain.
examples.professional: The brochure photo shows a turbaned guide leading the group through the old fort.
examples.analytical: The painting's turbaned figure signals the sitter's rank in the court portraiture of that period.

nuance.analogy: A turbaned head is like a head with a long scarf wrapped tightly around it, forming a crown of cloth.
nuance.etymology: Turban comes from Turkish tülbend, from Persian dulband.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as tur-BAN, when the stress is on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the d as a separate syllable, as tur-ban-ed.

senses.definition: To make a non-linear physical movement.
senses.example: the Earth turns

senses.definition: To move about an axis through itself.
senses.example: the Earth turns

senses.definition: To change the direction or orientation of, especially by rotation.
senses.example: Turn the knob clockwise.

senses.definition: To change one's direction of travel.
senses.example: She turned right at the corner.

senses.definition: To shape (something) symmetrically by rotating it against a stationary cutting tool, as on a lathe.
senses.example: She turned the table legs with care and precision.

senses.definition: To give form to; to shape or mold; to adapt.
To direct or impel (something) into or out of a place.
senses.example: Add sugar and butter, then turn the mixture into a dish.

senses.definition: To position (something) by folding it, or using its folds.
senses.example: turn the bed covers; turn the pages

senses.definition: To navigate through a book or other printed material.
senses.example: turn to page twenty; turn through the book

senses.definition: To twist or sprain.
senses.example: I fell off my bike and turned my ankle severely.

senses.definition: To change condition or attitude. To become.
senses.example: The leaves turn brown in autumn.

senses.definition: To become.
senses.example: The leaves turn brown in autumn.

senses.definition: To change the color of the leaves in the autumn.
senses.example: The hillside behind our house isn't generally much to look at, but once all the trees turn it's gorgeous.

senses.definition: To change fundamentally; to metamorphose.
senses.example: Midas made everything turn to gold. He turned into a monster every full moon.

senses.definition: To sour or spoil; to go bad.
senses.example: This milk has turned; it smells awful.

senses.definition: To make acid or sour; to ferment; to curdle.
senses.example: to turn cider or wine

senses.definition: To change (a person) into a vampire, werewolf, zombie, etc.
senses.example: How long ago was he turned?

senses.definition: To transform into a vampire, werewolf, zombie, etc.
senses.example: Bruce Banner turns when he is angry: he becomes the Hulk, an incredibly powerful green monster.

senses.definition: To change the sexual orientation or gender of another person, or otherwise awaken a sexual preference.
To hinge; to depend.
senses.example: The decision turns on a single fact.

senses.definition: To rebel; to go against something formerly tolerated.
senses.example: The prisoners turned on the warden.

senses.definition: To change personal condition.
senses.example: The sight turned my stomach.

senses.definition: To change personalities, such as from being a face (good guy) to heel (bad guy) or vice versa.
To make or become giddy; said of the head or brain.
To sicken; to nauseate.
senses.example: The sight turned my stomach.

senses.definition: To be nauseated; said of the stomach.
To change one's course of action; to take a new approach.
To complete.
senses.example: They say they can turn the parts in two days.

senses.definition: To make (money); turn a profit.
senses.example: We turned a pretty penny with that little scheme.

senses.definition: Of a player, to go past an opposition player with the ball in one's control.
To undergo the process of turning on a lathe.
senses.example: Ivory turns well.

senses.definition: To bring down the feet of a child in the womb, in order to facilitate delivery.
To magically or divinely repel undead.
To carve vegetables into uniform barrel-like or American football-like shapes.
senses.example: The hardest part of culinary school was learning to turn vegetables perfectly.

senses.definition: Of a bowler, to make (the ball) move sideways off the pitch when it bounces.
Of a ball, to move sideways off the pitch when it bounces.
(dated) To invert a type of the same thickness, as a temporary substitute for any sort which is exhausted.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A change of direction or orientation.
senses.example: Give the handle a turn, then pull it.

senses.definition: A movement of an object about its own axis in one direction that continues until the object returns to its initial orientation.
A unit of plane angle measurement based on this movement.
A walk to and fro.
senses.example: Let's take a turn in the garden.

senses.definition: A chance to use something shared in sequence with others.
senses.example: They took turns playing with the new toy.

senses.definition: A spell of work, especially the time allotted to a person in a rota or schedule.
senses.example: I cooked tonight, so it's your turn to do the dishes.

senses.definition: One's chance to make a move in a game having two or more players.
A figure in music, often denoted ~, consisting of the note above the one indicated, the note itself, the note below the one indicated, and the note itself again.
The time required to complete a project.
senses.example: They quote a three-day turn on parts like those.

senses.definition: The transition from one period or era, or hour on the clock, to another.
senses.example: turn of the century

senses.definition: A fit or a period of giddiness.
senses.example: I've had a funny turn.

senses.definition: A change in temperament or circumstance.
senses.example: She took a turn for the worse.

senses.definition: The fourth communal card in Texas hold 'em.
A deed done to another; an act of kindness or malice.
senses.example: One good turn deserves another.

senses.definition: A single loop of a coil.
A pass behind or through an object.
Character; personality; nature.
An instance of going past an opposition player with the ball in one's control.
A short skit, act, or routine.
A sideways movement of the ball when it bounces (caused by rotation in flight).
(dated) A type turned upside down to serve for another character that is not available.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To move so that you face or point in a different direction, or to rotate around a fixed axis.

pronunciation.tip: Use the r-colored vowel /ɜɹ/ in one syllable: keep the tongue relaxed and curl the r without adding an extra vowel like 'tur-un'. End with a clear n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a movement or change of direction with no positive or negative shading.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use turn constantly for physical movement (turn left, turn the key) and for taking a sequence or chance (it's your turn). It is natural in every setting. In phone and meeting talk, 'Can you turn that down?' is a common polite request about volume.

distinctions.note: Rotate is more technical and suggests continuous, full circular motion, as with a wheel or the Earth; turn can be a partial movement and is everyday.
Spin implies fast, repeated rotation; you turn a doorknob but you spin a top.
Twist implies bending or wringing an object out of shape, often with the hands; turn keeps the object's shape.

examples.everyday: Turn left at the gas station, and the store is on your right.
examples.professional: Can you turn the projector a little toward the window so the slide isn't washed out?
examples.analytical: The argument turns on a single assumption: that moral agents can act without any intention.

nuance.analogy: Like a door swinging on its hinge.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tyrnan, from Latin tornare, 'to turn on a lathe'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable and saying 'tur-en' instead of one syllable with a clear r.
Confusing 'turn to' (go to someone for help) with 'turn into' (become).
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew shuv (שׁוּב) means to turn back or return, and in religious use it means repentance. The Greek epistrephō (ἐπιστρέφω) means to turn toward, and in the New Testament it often means conversion. Ezekiel 18:32 has God calling people to turn back from their wrongdoing and live. Acts 3:19 calls hearers to repent and turn again so that their sins may be blotted out. Matthew 18:3 says that unless people turn and become like children they will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

senses.definition: Tweezers.
senses.example: The jeweler's tweezer set included three tips of different shapes and sizes.

senses.definition: A pair of tweezers, tweezers.
To use tweezers.
senses.example: He tweezered the stray hairs from his eyebrows before the wedding photos.
